en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Introduction to the Path of Purification:

This treatise called the *Visuddhimagga* (Path of Purification) is the very essence of the Three Pitakas, and among all books that illuminate the practice throughout the entire world, it is the foremost.
It is praised by the wise as being foremost, best, preeminent, chief, supreme, and excellent.

For herein, having condensed the meaning of the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Pitakas as established in the three councils, the holy life (*brahmacariya*) comprised within the three trainings is fully and clearly elucidated. Of this *Visuddhimagga*, thus praised—
There must certainly be an introductory narrative (*nidānakathā*) as well. Therefore, for the purpose of clarifying this matter, the following inquiry is stated:

"By whom was this *Visuddhimagga* composed? When was it composed? Where was it composed? Why was it composed? For what purpose was it composed? On what basis was it composed? In what manner was it composed?

And by whom is it spread throughout the entire world? Regarding these questions: "By whom was it composed? It was composed by the eminent Elder Ācariya Buddhaghosa, the author of the commentaries on the Tipiṭaka.
When was it composed? It was composed in the tenth century after the Parinibbāna of our Blessed One, the Sammasambuddha, the Lord of the Entire World (in the year 973 of the Buddhist Era).
Where was it composed? It was composed at the Mahāvihāra in Anurādhapura on the island of Sīhaḷa.

Why was it composed? It was composed because the Elder Saṅghapāla was moved by his own aspiration—namely, the desire to make known the method of right practice, which is the means for attaining purity—to virtuous people who long for purification, and because he was requested to do so by them.
Having established this point, the life story of the Venerable Ācariya Buddhaghosa Thera must now be told.

This account is indeed set forth in thirty-two verses, beginning from the one hundred and seventy-fifth verse (37, 215) in the thirty-seventh chapter of the *Mahāvaṃsa* (also known as the second part, the *Cūḷavaṃsa*). How so?—
In the vicinity of the Seat of Enlightenment,
there was born a young brahmin, a master of sciences, arts,
and crafts, who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas.
He who had correctly understood the right time, being confident in all doctrines,
was a proponent wandering through Jambudvīpa seeking debate.
Having approached a certain monastery, at night [he studied] the Pātañjala doctrine.
He turned it over, making the words complete and perfectly rounded.
There, a great elder named Revata, having understood, thought:
"This being possesses great wisdom; it is fitting to tame him."
“Who is it that brays with the cry of a donkey?
he asked. “What do you know about the meaning of the donkeys' braying?
he said to him. When told, “I know,” he set forth his own view.
He answered each question as it was asked and even demonstrated what had been missed.
When challenged with the words, "In that case,
you must uphold your own doctrine," he recited the *Abhidhamma* text but did not grasp its meaning.
He asked, "Whose spell is this? and he replied, "It is the Buddha-spell.
When [the king] said, "Give this to me," he [the Elder] said, "Take it by going forth into homelessness.
Desiring the spell, he went forth and mastered the Three Baskets (Piṭakattaya).
"This is the one-way path," he later declared.
Because of his profound voice, which was like that of a Buddha, they proclaimed him "Buddhaghosa";
for on this earth, his voice was like that of a Buddha.
In this regard, the treatise known as the *Ñāṇodaya* is not seen anywhere now; having composed that treatise, he then made the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*, which is the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
As for the *Aṭṭhasālinī* currently being seen, it is indeed of the island of Siṃhala (Ceylon), not of Jambudīpa; this will become clear later on pages 54–55.

Furthermore, by "Paritta-aṭṭhakathā" is meant the *Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā*, which is intended here as the concise commentary on the meaning of the Three Piṭakas; the wise one began to compose it among the various realms of existence.
Seeing this, the Elder Revata spoke these words:
"Only the canonical text (pāḷi) has been brought here; there is no commentary (aṭṭhakathā) here.

Why is it that the root commentary—which was received from the presence of the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa and transmitted through a succession of disciples and grand-disciples—has completely disappeared from Jambudīpa?"
It should be considered whether [the texts] have disappeared;
likewise, there exist no differing versions of the Teacher’s words.
The Sinhalese commentary is pure, brought by the wise Mahinda.
Having examined the path of discourse, including the Three Councils as they were recited, the teachings of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the songs sung by Sāriputta and others,
this [work] has been composed in the Sinhalese language and is current among the people of Siṃhala.
“Having gone there and heard it, you should translate it into the vernacular of the Magadhans;
that will be for the benefit of the whole world. When this was said, he became inspired with faith and, departing from there, [recited] this:
"He came to Dīpa at this very time, at this very [year]" refers to the period of King Mahānāma, from the 953rd to the 975th year of the Buddha era.

This chronological division is presented based on the *Sīhaḷa-rāja-vaṃsa*; however, according to the opinion of European scholars, it should be understood as being from the 941st to the 964th year of the Buddha era.
The same applies to the subsequent periods during the reign of King Mahāmati.
Having arrived at the Mahāvihāra, the monastery of all that is most excellent,
he went to the Great Hall of Exertion (Mahāpadhānaghara) into the presence of Saṅghapāla.
There he heard the Sinhalese commentary and the entire Theravāda in its entirety.
Having decided, "This indeed is the intention of the Dhamma itself," he gathered the Saṅgha there and said, "In order to compose a commentary,
give me all the manuscripts," so that he might examine them.
The Saṅgha gave him two verses: “Since you have the capability, show it here;
having seen it, we shall all give [the gift],” as stated in the manuscript. Regarding these two verses (234–5), this is the construction of the meaning:
“There, having led the Saṅgha to the Mahāvihāra and having caused the assembly of the Saṅgha to convene, the teacher Pubbaddhaghosa spoke thus.”
‘Give me all the manuscripts of the Pāḷi and its commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) so that I may compose a commentary.
To test him, the Saṅgha gave him two verses from the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*: “*Antojaṭā*,” etc., and “*Sīle patiṭṭhāya*,” etc.
This was done to demonstrate his capability and the power of his wisdom. Having seen this, [they gave him] all the manuscripts.

By this [statement], however, the following meaning is shown: “The teacher Buddhaghosa, while composing the *Visuddhimagga*, composed it after consulting only those two verses, without consulting any other manuscript whatsoever.
An investigation as to whether that claim is appropriate or not will follow later (on pages 39–49).
Having condensed the Three Baskets together with their commentaries,
he composed the work known as the *Visuddhimagga* (The Path of Purification) in brief. Then,
having convened the Saṅgha, which was well-versed in the doctrine of the Fully Enlightened One...
Near the Mahābodhi tree, he began to recite it.
To reveal his cleverness to the great multitude, the deities concealed the manuscript;
he did this two or three times. This is the meaning of that verse: “The deities...”

In order to demonstrate to the great multitude the skill and the flow of subtle wisdom of that Buddhaghosa, they covered the manuscript of the *Visuddhimagga* he had written, concealing it so that it became invisible;
yet Buddhaghosa wrote it a second time, and the deities covered that one as well; he wrote it for a third time as well. Thus it was said.

It was stated, "He did it two or three times"; relying on this very statement from the *Mahāvaṃsa* and expanding upon it, the story titled "The Origin of Buddhaghosa" explains how the *Visuddhimagga* was completed after being written three times in a single night.
Such a story, moreover, would surely produce wonder even among many discerning scholars.
It gives rise to doubt; therefore, this investigation will also be shown later (on pages 47–8).
When the manuscript was brought forth for recitation during the third session, the gods established two other manuscripts there as well.
Then the monks recited the three books together—
either according to the text or the meaning, or by way of their sequence from beginning to end;
whether by the words of the Elders' teachings, or by the canonical texts, or by the phrases and syllables.
There was no variation whatsoever even in the three sets of books.
Then the Saṅgha, exceedingly joyful and delighted, proclaimed again and again: "Without a doubt, this is Metteyya!"
Taking the commentaries along with the three Piṭakas,
while residing in the monastery known as Dūrasaṅkara,
he then recited all the Sinhalese commentaries from memory.
In the Magadha language, which is the root tongue of all beings and brings benefit to speakers of every tongue,
all the teachers of the Elders received that [Canon] as they would the Pāḷi itself.
"Then, when the duties to be performed had reached completion, he went to Jambudīpa to pay homage to the Great Bodhi.
This statement, "he went to Jambudīpa to pay homage to the Great Bodhi," seems as though it were unconnected to the preceding statements;
for previously it was said: "The teacher Buddhaghosa, near the Seat of Enlightenment..."

It is said: "He was born," and it is further stated: "Having gone to the island of Siṃhala, you must translate the Siṃhalese commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) into the Māgadhī language"—thus he was addressed by his teacher, the Elder Revata.
Therefore, the conduct of the teacher Buddhaghosa here is also consistent with that [instruction], as expressed in such passages as:
"Taking those commentaries translated into various languages, he went to Jambudīpa for the purpose of illuminating the Dispensation (*sāsana*)."
It ought to be rooted solely in the illumination of the Dispensation (*sāsana*), and not in the worship of the Great Bodhi tree.

Furthermore, regarding this narrative from the *Mahāvaṃsa*, it is stated in the introductory remarks to the *Visuddhimagga* manuscript printed in Roman script by the Hābadama Vidyālaya Press in the year 1950: "There are many points here that require investigation."

Having been spoken, this was investigated by the discerning Dhammānanda Kosambī. Having demonstrated here the examination of what is logical and illogical therein, we shall also conduct a further investigation of it.
This is the investigation of birth and lineage.

1. For there, that Dhammānanda, having stated, "It is not logical to say that Buddhaghosa was born near the Seat of Enlightenment (at Buddhagayā)," presented four counter-arguments (*vyatireka-kāraṇa*) to prove that point.
How so? (Ka) The first argument presented was: "Among the contemporary events elucidated by Buddhaghosa, not even one occurred in Magadha.
That is no reason at all. For the Venerable Master Buddhaghosa...
While composing the *Saṅgaha-ṭīkā*, he did so by condensing the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) themselves and distinguishing them merely by changing the language;
he did not do so by showing whatever he had personally seen or heard. For this was said by the Teacher:
“Commencing that commentary...”
Having made the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* its body,
and likewise the *Mahā-paccarī*,
which is renowned under names such as the *Kurundi*.
The exposition as stated in the commentaries,
which does not abandon the most appropriate meaning, and furthermore,
that which contains the doctrine of the Elders—
“I shall properly undertake this commentary,” thus [ends] the eighth [chapter], the introduction to the work and the discourse on commencing the book.
Then, having set aside other languages and having condensed the path of detailed exposition:
Having left out nothing of the entire *Vinicchaya*,
and without deviating in the slightest from the sequence of the *Tanti*,
[I shall explain] the meaning of the words of the *Suttanta*.
Since this commentary will also be elucidated in accordance with the suttas, it should therefore be studied with careful attention.
Thus ends the eighth [chapter], the Introduction to the Book. And here ends the introductory discourse on the composition of the work.
Just as the Master Buddhaghosa did not include contemporary Māgadhī historical accounts in his own commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*),
he likewise omitted those from Sīhaḷa and South India. For therein,
no events occurring after the time of King Vasabha (609–653 BE) are found, with the sole exception of the account concerning King Mahāsena.
In the *Pārāyaṇa* (Aṭṭha. 2.236–237), it is stated that the teacher arrived in the island of Siṃhala during the time of King Mahānāma, some three hundred years later [than the Buddha].
Therefore, one cannot conclude from the mere fact that the Magadhan dialects of that period are not clearly explained in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that [the language] was not Magadhan.

[Kha] Furthermore, he has presented a second reason, stating: "In all the works of Buddhaghosa, there is no exposition that makes [the subject] as clear as if it were seen directly through the power of the higher faculties (*uttarindriya*).
The fact that this too is not a valid reason is to be understood from the previous statement alone. Moreover, in the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*,...
It should also be understood from the commentary provided in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*. For therein it says:

"Just as one must go from the banks of the Kalamba River to the Thūpārāma by way of the gate of the Royal Mother’s Monastery, so too is the Sālavana Garden from the opposite bank of the river named Hiraññavatī. As [is the case] for Anurādhapura..."
“Thus it was with Kusinārā and the Thūpārāma. From the Thūpārāma, the road entering the city by the southern gate went eastward and then turned northward;
likewise, from the garden, the row of sāla trees went eastward and then turned northward.
Therefore, it is called ‘Upavattana’ (the Place of the Northward Turn),” as stated in *Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* 1.1.186 and *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* 2.198.
An exposition that appears as if it were seen through direct personal experience is indeed observed; however,

that too should be understood as being merely a transformation of language from the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), since such an explanation of the meaning must have been spoken from the time of the Elder Mahāmahinda himself.
Furthermore, after explaining the commentary stated in the *Visuddhimagga* (p. 30) as: "Regarding 'heat' (*uṇha*), it refers to the heat of fire;
its occurrence should be understood in forest fires and the like," and then having disparaged it by saying, "Moreover, its being beyond ridicule is quite evident," [the author] states:
"In the northern regions of the kingdom of India, during the summer season, [people] are without clothing..."
"The human skin is entirely scorched by the heat of the sun, yet those from the region of Dakkhiṇāpatha do not know this"—
this third reason is shown with greater emphasis. In that context,
if the statement "it is entirely scorched by the heat of the sun" were spoken directly with reference to being burnt specifically by the heat of the sun's rays, then [the following would apply]:

Regarding the phrase "the contact of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping things," it is not appropriate [to interpret "heat" (*ātapo*)] because it shares the same meaning as the word *ātapo*.
However, if it were said with reference to the state of being scorched by the hot element produced by the sun's heat,
then in that case, [it would apply] to the regions of the northern continent and other such extremely hot places where the heat produced by the sun's glare occurs.
The point that one makes use of robes and lodgings for the sake of warding off cold and heat is not unreasonable;
for it is said in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* (3.58):
"‘Cold and heat’ is stated by way of the discordance of the seasons (*utu-visabhāga*)."
Furthermore, that word-by-word commentary on the *Visuddhimagga* may have been derived from the ancient commentaries on the Suttantas.
For it is said in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, in the explanation of the *Sabbāsava Sutta* (I, 58):
"And here, 'heat' should be understood as the heat of fire; however, this instance [is given] by way of the heat of the sun."

...it is said. And here, if this matter had been stated by the Teacher according to his own opinion, he would have clarified that the point was already stated in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), as well as the fact that his own commentary on its meaning was based on his own opinion and was appropriate.
For wherever the Teacher demonstrates a specific point not mentioned in the ancient commentaries, [he does so explicitly].
In various places, such indicative statements are indeed made; for example, in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* (I, 72):

"In this case, the applications of *āṇattiya*, *nissaggiya*, and *thāvara* are also applicable, but since they have not been mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), they should be adopted after careful investigation";
and as it says in the *Papañcasūdanī* (I, 30): "This has not yet been investigated."
This statement, "But this [is] my own opinion," is not presented here as an authoritative pronouncement (*ñāpakavacana*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the statements, "‘Heat’ means the heat of fire" and "and here ‘heat’ should be understood as the heat of fire itself," are the words of the ancient commentary on the Suttantas (*porāṇasuttantaṭṭhakathāvacana*).
(Gha) Furthermore, while commenting on the Gopālaka Sutta in the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* titled *Papañcasūdanī* (Ma.
Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.350), Buddhaghosa seems to believe that "there are sandbanks in the middle of the river Gaṅgā between the kingdoms of Magadha and Videha. However, the Gaṅgā seen by Buddhaghosa...

The fourth reason shown is: "In the island of Sīhaḷa, it was indeed the Mahāveliganga [that was so], and not the Mahāgaṅgā, which is considered the best among the rivers of the Indiya kingdom"; this matter is indeed well known.
However, since one does not see such an island at that spot in the middle of the present-day Mahāgaṅgā, one must conclude with certainty that "it must have been exactly like this in the past."
This is merely what has been stated. However, since the rivers remain in that very same form at all times, it is impossible to grasp them;

thus, this meaning is indeed self-evident. Therefore, just as such islands were found in the middle of the Ganges at that place during the time of that cowherd previously, so too has this matter been described in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
And that very statement was explained by the Teacher after performing a change of linguistic expression; it should be understood exactly in this way.
Therefore, that too is indeed not a valid reason.
[End of] The Examination of the Brahmin Family.
2. Then, he also reflected thus upon the phrase "brahmin youth":
(Ka) "It cannot be taken for granted that Buddhaghosa was born into a brahmin family. Why? Because from the time of the Vedas until the present day, all those who are brahmins have [recited]:
'The Brahmin’s mouth was [his] origin; his arms became the Rājanya.'"
“His mouth was the Brāhmaṇa, from his arms the Rājanya was born,” as stated in the Ṛgveda, Maṇḍala 10, Hymn 90; likewise in the Atharvaveda, Book 6, Hymn 19, Verse 6.
One should have faith that they know this mantra called the *Purisa-sutta*.

Its meaning, however, is as follows: “The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms—that is to say, the Kṣatriyas were his arms; he who is the Vaiśya was his thighs; the Śūdra was born from his feet.”
However, even though Buddhaghosa was known as a "wise Brahmin," he did not know this verse.
For instance, in his commentary on the phrase *bandhupādāpaccā*, he states: "It is said that this is their doctrine:
Brahmins emerged from the mouth of Brahmā, Kshatriyas from his chest, Vaishyas from his navel, Shudras from his thighs, and Shramanas from the soles of his feet" (Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā).
"1.263; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.508: 'The meaning of that verse on knowledge (vedagāthā) has been described as not being identical [to this one].

Now, here is the investigation: if the view of the Brahmins of that time were exactly as stated in this verse, then that commentary on the meaning would be merely the opinion of the teacher. This being so, that..."
It should be considered as follows. However, in this verse, the meaning that "Brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahmā" cannot be obtained directly from the first line, "The Brahmin was his mouth.
But during the time of the Buddha, the view of the Brahmins was precisely that "Brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahmā"; thus, this meaning is indeed evident. Likewise...
For it is said in the *Aggañña Sutta* of the *Pāṭika Vagga* in the *Dīgha Nikāya* (3.67):
“Furthermore, Vāseṭṭha, one sees among the brahmins brahmin women who are menstruating, those who are pregnant, those who are giving birth, and those who are nursing.
And yet, although these brahmins are born from a womb just like others, they say: ‘The brahmin caste alone is the best;’”
“Other castes are inferior. Only the brahmin caste is fair; other castes are dark. Only brahmins are purified, not non-brahmins.
Only brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his breast, born from his mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, and heirs of Brahmā.
Thus they misrepresent Brahmā and speak falsehoods, producing much demerit.
The Blessed One, the Greatly Compassionate One, spoke these words to the young brahmin students Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, and they rejoiced in them.
Now, both of those students were pure by birth as brahmins and had mastered the three Vedas.
Therefore, [regarding] the statement, "Brahmins emerged from the mouth of Brahmā,"...
The fact that this was stated according to the tenets of the Brahmins of that time is indeed well known.

And just as this is so, one should believe that the statement, "Khattiyas from the chest, Vessas from the navel, Suddas from the feet, and Samaṇas from the back of the feet," was also spoken by the ancient commentators who knew the tenets of the Brahmins of that time; thus it was accepted by Master Buddhaghosa.
Everything [in this work] would have been explained as nothing more than a mere linguistic adaptation from the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
Therefore, even by means of that verse on knowledge (*vedagāthā*), the proof of the teacher’s non-Brahmin status remains entirely untenable.
(Kha) Furthermore, for the purpose of proving the non-Brahmin status of the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa, he brought forward a second reason as follows:
In the Brāhmaṇa texts, the word *bhrūṇahatī*, meaning the destruction of an embryo, appears in the Pāli Canon as *bhūnahu* (or *bhūnahano*). In the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta,
referring to the Magaṇḍiya wanderer’s role in destroying the embryo that ought to have arisen due to his wife’s lack of sexual intercourse,
the Magaṇḍiya wanderer addresses the Blessed One as “*bhūnahu* (or *bhūnahano*), the ascetic.”
"Gotama," etc., says the *Madhuratthavilāsinī* (MAṬ) 2.207 and so forth. It is evident from its commentary on that passage that Buddhaghosa was unaware of this;
for therein he explains the word *bhūnahanoti* as "one who kills beings, one who establishes a boundary [of slaughter]" (MAṬ 2.207).
That too is quite inappropriate. For Māgaṇḍiya did not speak of the state of being a destroyer of beings (bhūnahubhāva) with reference merely to the non-enjoyment of the object of touch;
rather, he spoke with reference to the non-enjoyment of all six objects of worldly gratification. For in that sutta it is said:
"Māgaṇḍiya, the eye delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and exults in forms; that [eye] has been subdued by the Tathāgata."
“He guards, protects, and restrains [his senses], and he teaches the Dhamma for their restraint;

was it with reference to this that you said of me, Māgaṇḍiya, ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer’? “Indeed, Master Gotama, it was precisely with reference to this that I said of you, ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer. For what reason? Because it accords with our own suttas. … [and so on] …
“The mind, Māgandiya, delights in the Dhamma, rejoices in the Dhamma, and finds joy in the Dhamma;
it is the Tathāgata’s mind, which is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained, and for its restraint he teaches the Dhamma.
Was it with reference to this, Māgandiya, that you said, ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer’? Indeed, Master Gotama, it was precisely with reference to this that I spoke.”
“The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings. For what reason? Because it is thus that he descends into our discourses (sutta), as stated in M.N. 2.207 and elsewhere.
Thus, both the Blessed One’s inquiry and Māgandiya’s response have come down.
For herein, it is specifically due to the enjoyment of the object of touch by way of engaging in sexual intercourse that conception occurs.
The term "destroyer of beings" (*bhūnahū*) is rightly applied with reference specifically to the non-enjoyment of that [fetus];

however, for the other five objects—form and so forth—and particularly for the object of mental phenomena (*dhammārammaṇa*), there is no cause for enjoyment by pure mind-consciousness (*suddhamanoviññāṇa*) once the conception has been established.
Therefore, it is called a "destroyer of beings" with reference to their non-enjoyment.
It is certainly not appropriate to say so; however, Māgaṇḍiya has admitted that he spoke with reference to all of them, and he has provided the reason:

"For it is thus that [the word] descends into our Sutta. Therefore, although the word *bhūnahu* (*bhrūnahā*) is seen in the Brahmanical texts in the sense of killing an embryo, in the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta this meaning [is intended].

It should be understood that by the Master [Buddhaghosa] stating "it is not logical," this very meaning—that he is one who has destroyed growth and established a boundary—is expressed through a change of language from the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
(Ga) Furthermore, by him [the opponent], it was said: "This, moreover, is the final reason proving that Buddhaghosa is not a Brahmin."
For in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the Description of Virtue (Sīlaniddesa, 1.31), while making a jest with the brahmins, [the Blessed One] said: "In this way, by partaking of almsfood,
I shall ward off both the old feeling of hunger and prevent the arising of a new feeling caused by excessive eating—
such as that of the *āharahatthaka*, the *alaṃsāṭaka*, the *tatravaṭṭaka*, the *kākamāsaka*, or the *bhuttavamitaka* brahmins."
He said, "One practices with the thought, 'I shall not produce [anger] as if it were [already] produced. However, this might also be the statement of a certain Brahmin who held a divergent view;
making that very point the firm reason, one cannot say, "Buddhaghosa was not a Brahmin.
This third reason was stated. But that is indeed a most deeply moving statement. For this was not said by the Master [the Buddha] regarding the Brahmins...
This was spoken by one wishing to joke, yet it is not a matter that should be connected with a humorous remark;
rather, it is a matter to be spoken for the purpose of exhortation and instruction to fellow celibates by demonstrating the state of things as they truly are.
And so it was spoken by the Teacher. For there are in the world certain ascetics or brahmins who subsist on what is given by others...

Or other persons as well—devoid of the knowledge of reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) and established in non-restraint—might occasionally, having obtained an abundance of extremely refined food, consume it in measureless quantities.

In particular, it is well known that Brahmins were such individuals, both by way of worldly matters and by way of the canonical accounts in the *Jātaka* and other texts. For in this world, after a hundred thousand years...
Or for tens of millions of years, or for an immeasurable duration—who could say, "It was never thus before"?
Therefore, it was stated precisely as an introduction to the instruction and admonition that one should not be like those who consume food in unlimited quantities.
Thus, although it was indeed beneficial in meaning, for one who attends to it improperly, it resulted only in harm, just as in the case of [the monk] with his wife.
The verses taught for the sake of the non-returner path and its fruit to the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya—found in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, Sāmāvatī-vatthu, verse 8—resulted in harm to his daughter;
therefore, in this case, only a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) should be cultivated.
*Patañjali-vāda-vicāraṇā* (An Examination of the Doctrine of Patañjali)
3. Now, that statement, “he refutes the system of Patañjali,” was also investigated in this way:
(Ka) “Buddhaghosa knew only a small portion of the doctrine of Patañjali or of others from the Uttaraindira kingdom.
For in the doctrines of Patañjali, he presented only these two [powers], *aṇimā* and *laghimā*, in Visuddhimagga 1.144.”
Not knowing the *Yogasūtra* that goes beyond that, and having weighed the doctrine of Patañjali, no such illumination is seen in his own books;

furthermore, neither the work composed by Patañjali nor even the mere name "Patañjali" is mentioned therein. However, in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the description of the plane of wisdom (*paññābhūmi-niddesa*), it says:
"Purity (*visuddhi*) is like the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of those who maintain the doctrine of primordial nature."
"2.584 Only the mere name *pakativāda* (the theory of primordial matter/theory of number) is revealed; and right there, in the *Visuddhimagga*, it is stated:
‘In the world, a member of a syllogism (*vacanāvayava*) such as ‘proposition’ (*paṭiññā*) or ‘reason’ (*hetu*) is called a *hetu*.

By this, it is known that Buddhaghosa knew only a small portion of the root text of the *Nyāya* treatise which elucidates the methods of the faculties and reasoning (*indriya-takkanaya*), and that he did not know it in its entirety."
But all of that is merely a total misrepresentation of the teacher.

For when one provides a commentary on the meaning of the Three Piṭakas—which are exceedingly profound, highly venerable, and perfectly pure—one must elucidate only such matters as the perfectly pure method of the Canon (pāḷi), the method of the Commentaries (aṭṭhakathā), and the doctrines of the ancient Elders; or else, whatever...
Worldly textual passages connected with grammatical analysis that are helpful for the commentary on the meaning should be explained as appropriate;
however, one need not explain even those things that are unhelpful, such as the names of various authors of those texts and the many words spoken by them.
For by not explaining these, it does not follow that "the commentator did not know them."

It should be said: for if he were to include and explain in his own commentary every worldly treatise he knew, even those that were of no benefit, it would become excessively prolix, impure, and disregarded by the wise followers of the Teaching;
thus it should be understood that the teacher did not explain the doctrines of Patañjali and others in detail.

In fact, whatever portions of worldly texts have been brought forward and explained by the Teacher, those very texts and others of a similar kind must be known by the wise simply as being recognized by the Teacher;
just as, upon seeing a portion of the ocean, the entire ocean is known to be like that. For wherever the Teacher [encountered] words connected with the Vedas...
They were brought forth by bringing various portions from the Vedic texts here and there.
For instance, in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, the Master states:
"‘Of the three Vedas’ means of the *Iruveda*, *Yajuveda*, and *Sāmaveda*” (Dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.256). And:

“‘With Itihāsa as the fifth’ means: having made the Atharva-veda the fourth, those for whom Itihāsa—which consists of ancient stories connected with such expressions as ‘Thus it was’ and ‘Thus it was’—is the fifth, are the ‘Itihāsa-fifth ones’;
[the phrase refers to] ‘of those Vedas which have Itihāsa as the fifth,’” according to Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā 1.256.
“*Iṭṭhaṃ* is said to mean a great sacrifice,” according to *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* 1.170–172;
and “*Agnihoma* means the offering into the fire, thinking: ‘When one sacrifices with such wood in this manner, this [result] occurs.
*Dabbihoma* and the like are also *agnihomas*, because they proceed in this way: ‘When one sacrifices with such a ladle (*dabbi*) using such grains (*kaṇa*) and so forth, this [result] occurs.’”
Furthermore, [the passage] “but they are mentioned separately” (Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.21),
and “[taking mustard seeds and other things with the mouth and throwing them into fire, or offering oblations after reciting a spell, is ‘mouth-oblation’]” (Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.21)—
such statements connected with the Vedas have been described in accordance with the Vedic texts. And these [statements] are from the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
They might also have been stated by way of a change in language; however, it is not easy for one unskilled in the Vedic texts to perform a literal translation of the language.
Therefore, the teacher’s proficiency in the Vedic texts was indeed manifest.
Thus, he was one who was truly well-versed both in the Vedic texts and in other worldly texts.
It should be understood that the reason for not providing a detailed exposition of these [points] is precisely the one already stated.
Furthermore, the Teacher himself, at the very commencement of his own work, states:
"And then, having set aside even another language..."
Having condensed the detailed path and having set forth the entire analysis without omission... [etc.
...for this commentary shall also come to be—thus ends the eighth [chapter], the Introduction to the Work.
Then, having removed the delightful Sinhalese language and having adapted it to be suitable for the methods of the discourses (Tanti) and free from defects,
I did not violate the tradition of the Elders, who are the lamps of the lineage of the Elders.

“Having set aside the works of those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra who possess subtle discernment, I shall elucidate the meaning of the matter that has come down repeatedly. Thus ends the introductory discourse on the composition of the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*.
And so, having distinguished the new commentaries by means of both the translation of the language and the condensation [of the old ones], the ancient commentaries...
It should also be understood that after promising "I shall do so," he acted exactly as promised, rather than having distinguished himself through the power of his own knowledge.
Therefore, regarding the lack of detailed exposition of the *Patañjalivāda* and other works in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*),
the statement that "Buddhaghosa did not know the *Patañjalivāda* and others thoroughly" is merely a slander against the Master.
Investigation of the Kāvya Treatises 4.

Furthermore, he said this: "Although Buddhaghosa does not appear to be as highly skilled in the great kāvya treatises known as the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, nevertheless, he did demonstrate them. How so? 'Narratives' refers to the battle of the Bhāratas and so forth."
"Furthermore, it is shown in the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* 1.13 that one should not even go to the place where such talk is being held;

and in the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā* 1.8, it is shown that there are two constituent factors for that [idle chatter]: the preoccupation with useless talk such as the Battle of the Bhāratas or the Abduction of Sītā, and the actual speaking of such talk."
Moreover, that [statement] is even more causeless than the previous one; it is merely an act of disrespect.

For what purpose would there be in providing a detailed exposition of the *kāvya* literature—which consists of a collection of meaningless, frivolous chatter—in a commentary on the meaning of the Three Piṭakas, which possess an exceedingly profound meaning and are of supreme importance?
On the contrary, such an act would only result in their being dishonored.
"And because of disrespect toward those who are wise. [This is] the fifth [point], the defilement of the quality of great learning.
Furthermore, Dhammānanda, wishing to defile the teacher’s quality of great learning, spoke thus: "Of him (Buddhaghosa)..."
"Scholarship renowned for proficiency in other systems is not superior to that of the modern Sīhaḷa bhikkhus who are proficient in various texts,
or to that of the bhikkhus such as Anuruddha and Dhammapāla who arose in South India during the eleventh century of the Christian era (1001–1100)."

That, however, is an entirely improper statement. For if either contemporary Sinhalese bhikkhus or ancient teachers such as the elders Ācariya Anuruddha and Dhammapāla were equal to or superior to Ācariya Buddhaghosa by virtue of their extensive knowledge of other systems,
they would have been dissatisfied with the commentaries of the elder Ācariya Buddhaghosa.
Having offered [this], they might then compose new commentaries that are more beautiful and more complete; however, they do not do so.
Not only do they not do so, but not even one among them says, "I am equal to Buddhaghosa by virtue of great learning," or "I am superior. On the contrary, they [speak] of their teacher...
The commentaries themselves both criticize and support [this view], and they establish it in the position of a teacher.
Therefore, it is known that this statement is entirely improper in every respect.
This concludes the investigation of the Mahāyāna method.
6. Furthermore, not being satisfied even with that much, he disparaged his teacher and said:
"I suspect Buddhaghosa does not know even the name, let alone the system, of those such as Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, who were the preeminent teachers of the Mahāyāna school.
However, that was merely a reprimand consisting of words that were utterly unrighteous and pointless.
For it cannot be said that he did not know the doctrines and methods of other schools simply because they were not explained in his own commentary.
Did the Master not state at the very beginning of the commentaries on the scriptures:
“Not violating the tradition of the Elders, who are the lamps of the lineage of the Elders...”
And: "Of those who dwell in the Mahāvihāra, whose discernment is most skillful.
And here too, in the *Visuddhimagga*:
"Based on the method of teaching of the residents of the Mahāvihāra..."
"I shall speak the *Visuddhimagga*," thus [it is] purity (*visuddhi*).

And: "By one composing a commentary on its meaning, having entered the circle of those who advocate analytical exposition (*vibhajjavāda*), not misrepresenting the teachers, not overstepping our own system, not importing foreign systems, and not contradicting the Suttas or the Vinaya..."
For the commentary on the meaning must be made by one who surveys the Great Authorities in direct order, who elucidates the Dhamma,
who compiles the meaning, and who, having repeated that very same meaning, demonstrates it further through other methods;
thus [it is said in the] *Visuddhimagga* (2.581).
“Since this Dispensation is adorned with various methods of teaching,
and the path of the ancient masters continues without interruption,
therefore, relying upon both of these, I shall provide this commentary on the meaning.”
“I shall begin this for the sake of purification.
Having given his promise, he composed the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) exactly in accordance with that promise. Thus, the reason for their composition must be explained here;
therefore, in order to clarify that, [the account] begins from the time of the Parinibbāna of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Up until the time of Ācariya Buddhaghosa, we shall also explain the sequence of the propagation of the Dispensation.
Regarding the sequence of the propagation of the Dispensation:
after the time of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, within the interval of one hundred years, there was no division of doctrine whatsoever in the Buddha-sāsana.

There was no [separate] name for it. However, at the time of the hundred-year [council], the Vajjiputta monks, having been expelled by the elders who presided over the Second Council, gained a following and, having altered the Dhamma and Vinaya, held a separate council known as the Mahāsaṅgīti.
At that time, for the elders who accepted only the ancient Dhamma and Vinaya as recorded in the two councils:
The group known as the Theravādins and those others are designated as the Mahāsaṅghikas.
Furthermore, from the Mahāsaṅghikas, two teacher-groups arose: (1) the Gokulikas and (2) the Ekavyāvahārikas.
Again, from the Gokulikas, two [groups] arose: (3) the Paññattivādins and (4) the Bāhulikas (or Bahussutikas). Moreover, from the Bāhulikas...
(5) Regarding the statement "the Cetiyavādin group arose": these five, together with the Mahāsāṅghika who served as their root, constituted six distinct teacher-groups (*ācariyagaṇa*).
From the pure Theravāda as well, two teacher-groups arose: (1) the Mahīśāsaka and (2) the Vajjiputtaka.
Furthermore, from the Mahīśāsaka, two more arose: (3) the Sabbatthivāda and (4) the Dhammaguttika. Again, from the Sabbatthivāda as well—
(5) Kassapīya; from that also (6) Saṅkantika; and from that also (7) Suttavādī—these three arose.
From the Vajjiputtakas also (8) Dhammuttariya, (9) Bhaddayānika, (10) Channāgārika, and (11) Sammitiya—these four arose.
Thus, together with the fundamental Visuddha-Theravāda, there were twelve schools of teachers. So it was.
These twelve schools and the six preceding ones—making eighteen groups of teachers—arose between the second and third councils.

Among them, the Theravāda group alone, being the fundamental one and holding the ancient Dhamma and Vinaya in high esteem, preserved the ancient Dhamma and Vinaya in its entirety, pure, complete, and without addition or omission.
The other seventeen schismatic groups, however, [did not preserve] the ancient...

They altered the Dhamma and Vinaya. Consequently, their Dhamma and Vinaya became deficient in some respects and excessive in others, and thus they were both incomplete and impure. Therefore, it is said in the fifth chapter of the *Dīpavaṃsa*:
“The Vajjiputtaka monks, those evil bhikkhus, were expelled by the Elders.”
Having gained another faction, many people who spoke what was not the Dhamma assembled in ten thousand and performed the compilation of the Dhamma;
therefore, this recitation of the Dhamma is called the "Great Recitation" (Mahāsaṅgīti).
The monks of the Great Council acted contrary to the Teaching;
having split the original compilation, they made another compilation.
They placed the discourses compiled in one place into another.
They split both the meaning and the Dhamma, regarding the Vinaya and the five Nikāyas... [as before] ...
They split both the meaning and the Dhamma, and they compiled only a portion;
for having discarded a portion of the texts, they composed something else.
Having abandoned their names, emblems, requisites, and customary practices,
as well as their natural disposition, they made themselves something else.
There were seventeen schools that split the doctrine, while the single school remained undivided.
All eighteen schools exist together with those who hold divergent views.
Yet the Elder [Nigrodha], like a great banyan tree, is supreme among those who proclaim the doctrine;
he teaches the teaching of the Conqueror in its entirety—neither deficient nor redundant.
Like thorns grown upon a tree, these remaining sects have arisen.
In the first century [after the Buddha’s passing], there were none;
in the second century, seventeen schools split off and appeared within the Jina’s dispensation. Thus ends the eighth discourse. This concludes the Nidānakathā.
In the time of King Aśoka, certain followers of other sects, having lost their gains and honor, went forth among the bhikkhus out of a desire for gain and honor.
They proclaimed their respective views, saying, "This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya; this is the Teacher’s instruction.
Even though they could not obtain the going-forth in the presence of the bhikkhus, they themselves shaved off their hair and put on saffron robes.
Having covered themselves, they wander about in the monasteries; when it is time for the performance of the Uposatha ceremony and other rites, they enter into the midst of the Saṅgha.

Even though they are being restrained by the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, they do not settle into a practice that conforms to the Dhamma and Vinaya, and they give rise to various kinds of sores, stains, and thorns for the Sāsana.
Some were worshipping fire; some were practicing austerities in the heat of five fires; some were circumambulating the sun;
and some, thinking "we shall split the Dhamma and the Vinaya," exerted themselves in various ways.
At that time, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus did not perform the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā ceremony together with them; for seven years, the Uposatha was suspended at the Asoka Monastery.
The Discourse on the Eight [Points]: The Nidānakathā; Pārāyanavagga: The Discourse on the Third Council.
Furthermore, with reference to this occurrence, it can also be understood thus:
"In the later times of the Dhamma and Vinaya, when the seventeen schools of schism had arisen, the state of being less pure came about through such causes as these."

For although the meaning—that within the perfectly pure Dhamma and Vinaya which constitute the Buddha’s teaching, there is nothing whatsoever that is permanent, stable, or eternal except for the element of Nibbāna; that in the ultimate sense there is no self (attā);

and that all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) are indeed impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and non-self—is exceedingly well-known, nevertheless, now, among those who hold the views of the elders (Theravādins)...

In the books and in the earlier Vetullavāda and other works, the meaning is seen [stated] thus: "The Buddha is permanent, stable, eternal, and the self," and "All sentient beings are also permanent, stable, eternal, and the self.
Then King Asoka, desiring to purify the Teaching, first [consulted] the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.
Having mastered the agreement, he brought together groups of monks who held the same views;
then, calling each group of monks one by one, he asked: "Venerable sirs, what is the doctrine of the Perfectly Enlightened One?

Thereupon, those who held the false views corresponding to their own respective doctrines—such as "The Perfectly Enlightened One is an eternalist" or "He is a partial-eternalist," and so forth—[spoke accordingly].
They said, "These are not those monks; these are followers of other sects. Having known this as it truly was, he gave them white garments and caused them to disrobe.
They numbered about sixty thousand in all.
Then, having questioned other monks, when they replied, "O Great King, the Fully Enlightened One is a proponent of analysis (vibhajjavādī)," [he thought: "Pure..."
"Venerable sir, now is the time for the teaching; let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus perform the Uposatha," he said, and having provided protection, he entered the city.
The Saṅgha, being in harmony, assembled and performed the Uposatha.
At that gathering, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, for the purpose of warding off all those matters that had arisen at that time and those that would arise in the future, [spoke].
Following the very method imparted by the Teacher, the Tathāgata himself,
he analyzed the matrix (mātikā) thus established and expounded the fifth treatise in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka called *Kathāvatthu*, which crushes the doctrines of others. Then,

one thousand monks of the Theravāda school— headed by the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, who were bearers of the Tipiṭaka tradition and had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)— [recited] that which had been set down in the two councils.
Having recited the pure, ancient Dhamma and Vinaya once again, they protected it well-guarded; thus there were eight [recitations].
1. The Discourse on the Third Council.
Then, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, for the purpose of establishing the Dispensation in the nine frontier regions, [sent forth] nine...

Having selected the leaders among the elders, he sent them forth. Among them, after eight elders had each gone to their respective places and established themselves in the Buddha’s dispensation, the Elder Mahinda, in the two hundred and thirty-sixth year (236) after the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, traveled from Jambudīpa to the island of Siṃhala.
There, he inspired faith in the multitude of people on the island, headed by King Devānampiyatissa.
He firmly established the Buddha’s dispensation; and having accepted the Mahāmeghavana garden granted by that king, he established there a monastic complex for the Saṅgha named the Mahāvihāra.
From that time forth, until the reign of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī, the Buddha’s dispensation on the island of Siṃhala remained free from the confusion of sectarian doctrines.
Having become stainless and perfectly pure, it blazed forth. From the time of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi onwards, however, proponents of other schools (nikāyantaravāda) also arrived on the island of Sri Lanka.

At that time, the Theravādins who were purified guarded that [tradition] with great effort so that it would remain well-protected, unmixed with those other sectarian doctrines, untarnished, and naturally pure, just as the ancient Dhamma and Vinaya had been. How so?
Regarding the Origin of the Abhayagirivihāra Nikāya:
King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī, having ascended the throne in the 425th year after the Buddha’s *parinibbāna*, was harassed for about five months by the Brahmin Tissa Dāmarika and seven Tamil warriors;
defeated in battle, he fled and [ruled] for more than fourteen years.
Having concealed himself in another guise, he dwelt [there], starting from the 37th verse of the 33rd chapter of the *Mahāvaṃsa*.
At that time, the people of the island of Laṅkā, being afflicted by the fear of thieves and the fear of famine, were unable to provide the four requisites for the monks;
consequently, most of the monks departed from there for Jambudīpa to [preserve] the Dhamma and Vinaya.

They dwell maintaining [the teachings]. Even those elders who remained behind on the island of Laṅkā, subsisting on whatever roots, tubers, and leaves they obtained, would sit upon the ground while their bodies were still strong and recite the scriptures;
when their strength failed, they would heap up sand, sit surrounded by it with their heads placed together in one spot, and contemplate the scriptures. In this manner, for twelve years...
They preserved the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries (*sāṭṭhakatha*) without losing anything. However, when King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi, having slain the Damila king,
re-established his reign once more— within the [period of] 455 to 466 years after the Buddha’s parinibbāna (Mahāvaṃsa 33.78)—
those elders, together with the elders who had returned from Jambudīpa, were purifying the Tipiṭaka, [ensuring it was] not even a single syllable...
They did not see [the text] called Asamaṇṭa (Aṭṭha. 1.130; Vibha. Aṭṭha. 810).

Furthermore, even that Mahāniddesa, which at that time was familiar only to a single immoral bhikkhu, was preserved by the Elder Mahātipiṭaka after he had the Elder Mahārakkhita learn it from him (Pārā.
Aṭṭha. 2.585). Thus, [it survived] despite the calamities of famine, civil unrest, and invasion.
Because they were oppressed, they carefully upheld the Dhamma and Vinaya even during a difficult period.
The king, having caused the monastery named Abhayagiri to be built, gave it to the Elder Mahātissa, who had previously rendered him assistance.
However, because that elder was excessively involved with worldly families, the monks residing at the Mahāvihāra performed an act of banishment against him.
Having done so, he was expelled. At that time, his disciple, the elder named Bahalamassutissa, opposed that formal act;
consequently, the Saṅgha performed an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) against him.
Becoming angry with the Mahāvihāravāsins, he went to the Abhayagiri Vihāra itself and, joining forces with the elder Mahātissa, lived there leading a separate faction. These two elders—
They did not return to the Mahāvihāra, as recorded in verses such as Mahāvaṃsa 33.79.
From that time forth, two schools arose in the island of Siṃhala: the Mahāvihāravāsins and the Abhayagirivāsins.
This, first of all, was the primary cause for the decline of the Sāsana in the island of Siṃhala.
The Origin of the Dhammaruci Nikāya:
At that time, the king, having become especially devoted to the monks residing at Abhayagiri, supported them alone by providing the four requisites;
likewise, many well-known persons, including royal ministers and others, did the same.
Having established many other monasteries besides that one, they gave them [to the monks].
Thus, the monks dwelling at Abhayagiri were honored, revered, and esteemed by many well-known people.

Furthermore, the Abhayagiri residents, such as the elder Mahāsīvatissa and others, [received] from the kingdom of India the community belonging to the Dhammaruci sect, which was included within the Vajjiputtaka group, who had arrived from there.
In the verses of the *Mahāvaṃsa* (33.99), it is stated that they accepted a new Piṭaka composed in the Pāli language and based on the Dhamma and Vinaya;
because of this, they became known as the Dhammaruci sect. This was the second cause for the decline of the Saṅgha in the island of Sri Lanka.
As for the transcription of the Three Piṭakas into books,
the residents of the Mahāvihāra accepted only the ancient, pure Piṭaka established in the Pāli language,
and they preserved it solely by means of oral recitation. However, at that time, the elders, observing the decline in the mindfulness and wisdom of later generations, [acted accordingly].
From the time of the Buddha until that period, they began to commit the Tipiṭaka, together with its commentaries,
to writing as it had been transmitted orally. While undertaking this task, they resided in the Ālokaleṇa cave in the city of Mātula (known today by the designation Mātale) in the Malayajanapada—
a region measuring sixty-eight *mīla*— situated before the royal capital of Anurādhapura, for the sake of one local [donor].
The rulers of the provinces took charge of the protection and carried out the work of transcribing the Tipiṭaka into books, as recorded in the verses at *Mahāvaṃsa* 33.100–101.

From this it is known that at that time, the elders residing at the Mahāvihāra, having received no assistance from the king or the royal ministers, performed the work of transcribing the Tipiṭaka into books solely by their own power; and that was exactly so for the sake of future generations.

"Having seen the decline of mindfulness and wisdom, it was composed; likewise, having seen its difficult-to-sustain nature during times afflicted by dangers such as famine and civil unrest," and similarly, "it was also composed so that the residents of Abhayagiri would not be confused by the doctrines accepted by other schools.
Thus, the elders of the Mahāvihāra [compiled] the pure Theravāda Piṭaka from among the various systems...
For the sake of preventing confusion, they preserved it well by having it inscribed in books in the Pāḷi language itself, just as it was before.

For if the Tipiṭaka had not been committed to books at that time, it would have been difficult in later ages to reject those suttas that arrived from other traditions, saying, "These are not ours. But since...
At that time, the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries was committed to books;
from that very fact, it became easy to verify and reject suttas that had appeared in other periods by cross-referencing them with those books.
For instance, during the reign of King Bhātika (524–552 BE), a dispute arose between the Mahāvihāravāsins and the Abhayagirivāsins regarding the Vinaya.
A dispute arose. At that time, the king dispatched a minister of Brahmin birth named Dīghakārāyaṇa to the presence of the Elders.
Having heard the arguments of both sides, he delivered a judgment in favor of the Theravādins. Likewise, during the reign of King Vohāratissa (c.
758–780 BE) and during the reign of King Goṭhābhaya (c. 797–810 BE), the Theravādins [established their authority] by means of the texts committed to writing.
Having compared it with the Dhamma and Vinaya, they rejected the discourse on what is not Dhamma (adhammavāda) at Nikāyasaṅgaha, page 12. Regarding the arising of the discourse on what is not Dhamma:
this is the origin, from the beginning, of those who speak what is not Dhamma, who constitute the defilement of the Dispensation. For during the time of King Asoka...
Having been expelled and driven out at an opportune time, those followers of other sects, finding no foothold in the Buddha’s teaching and overcome by anger, departed from Pāṭaliputta.
Gathering together at Nālandā near Rājagaha, they deliberated thus:
"In order that the great multitude may not penetrate the Buddha’s teaching, the Dhamma and Vinaya of the Sakyans must be destroyed; and furthermore—"
"Since it is not possible for those who do not know their own time [to act], one must therefore go forth there once again by whatever means possible.

Having deliberated thus, they returned; but being unable to enter among the proponents of the doctrine of the Elder Visuddha, they approached other groups, namely the seventeen schools such as the Mahāsāṅghikas.
Having gone forth without revealing his status as a follower of another sect, he mastered the Tipiṭaka and thoroughly mastered its recitation.
Then, having gone to Kosambī, he deliberated upon a means for the destruction of the Dhamma and Vinaya.

In the twenty-five hundred and third year of the Buddha’s parinibbāna, while residing in six locations—(1) Hemavatika, (2) Rājagirika, (3) Siddhatthika, (4) Pubbaseliya... [and so on]—he acted accordingly.
The Aparaselīyas (6), Vājiriyas (7), Vetullakas (8), Andhakas (9), and the Aññamahāsaṅghikas—these nine new schools arose, as stated on page 9 of the *Nikāyasaṅgraha*.

Their names and tenets are already recorded in the commentary to the *Kathāvatthu*. Among them, the Hemavatikas presented a counterfeit of the True Dhamma (*saddhammapatirūpaka*) by representing it as having been spoken by the Buddha.
(1) They composed the text known as the *Vaṇṇapiṭaka*.
The Rājagirikas [composed] the *Aṅgulimālapiṭaka*,
and the Siddhatthikas [composed] the *Gūḷhavessantara*.
The Pubbaseliyas (4) composed the Raṭṭhapālagajjita;
the Aparaseliyas (5) composed the Āḷavakagajjita;
and the inhabitants of Vajirapabbata composed the Vajiriyā (6), a text known as the Gūḷhavinaya.
They all likewise composed numerous *tantra* texts, such as the *Māyājālatantra* and the *Samājatant*, as well as numerous *kalpa* texts, such as the *Marīcikappakalpa* and the *Herambhakappakalpa*.
Furthermore, the Vetullavādins composed the *Vetullapiṭaka*,
while the Andhakas [composed] works such as the *Ratanakūṭa*.
And other Mahāsāṅghikas compiled suttantas such as the *Akkharasāri* into their ninefold collection of scriptures (*nikāya-saṅgaha*).
Among those [scriptures] which were mere counterfeits of the true Dhamma, only these three—the Vetullavāda, the Vājiriya-vāda, and the Ratana-kūṭa-sattha—reached the island of Laṅkā;
however, others, such as the Vaṇṇapiṭaka and so forth, remained only in Jambudīpa.
This is stated in the *Nikāyasaṅgaṇī*. Furthermore, the shadow of the *Vaṇṇapiṭaka* and other texts is indeed seen to have reached the island of Laṅkā.
For instance, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya (page 3, line 9), it says:
“The *Vaṇṇapiṭaka*, the *Aṅgulimālapiṭaka*, the *Raṭṭhapālagajjita*, the *Āḷavakagajjita*, the *Gūḷhamagga*, and the *Gūḷhavessantara*...”

Regarding the *Gūḷhavinaya* and the *Vedallapiṭaka*, it should be understood that here “*vepulla*, *vedallaṃ*, and *vetulla*” are synonymous terms, and they are simply names for the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*.
For it has been stated by the teacher named Asaṅga in his *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, a Mahāyāna treatise (page 79):
“What is *vepulla*? It is the teaching associated with the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*.”
That which is called *vepulla* is also called *vedalla* and *vetulla*. For what purpose is it called *vepulla*?
Because it is based on the welfare and happiness of all beings, and because it is a sublime and profound teaching of the Dhamma.
For what purpose is it called *vedalla*? Because it tears asunder all obscurations. For what purpose is it called *vetulla*? Because there is no comparison for its illustrative teachings.
And it is stated [in the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*] (vol. 2, p. 186):

“The *Gūḷhavinaya*, the *Gūḷhavessantara*, the *Gūḷhamahosadha*, the *Vaṇṇapiṭaka*, the *Aṅgulimālapiṭaka*, the *Raṭṭhapālagajjita*, the *Āḷavakagajjita*, and the *Vedallapiṭaka*—these are called non-Buddha-word, being mere counterfeits of the True Dhamma.”
The refutation of those [views] is seen. For it would not have been possible for the Sinhalese masters of the Aṭṭhakathās to refute them without having heard them or understood their meaning;
nor could that refuting statement be the word of the masters of the Jambudīpa Aṭṭhakathās, because they were non-existent at the time when the Elder Mahāmahinda departed for the island of Sri Lanka.
Therefore, it should be understood that those Mahāyāna Piṭakas and others belonging to that period were for the most part brought to the island of Siṃhala.
Regarding these, the arrival of the Piṭakas of the Dhammaruci school—which was included within the Vajjiputtaka group—has already been mentioned previously.
However, the arrival of the other [Mahāyāna texts] should be understood as follows.
The first suppression of the Vetullavāda occurred during the time of King Vohārakatissa (758–780 CE). At that time, members of the Dhammaruci sect residing at Abhayagiri,
by means of Brahmins who were proponents of the Vetullavāda wearing the guise of monks, composed [texts] for the purpose of destroying the Dispensation in the manner previously described.
Having accepted the Vetullapiṭaka, they presented it as "spoken by the Buddha.
The Mahāvihāravāsin Thervādins, having compared it with the Dhamma and Vinaya, rejected it as a teaching not in accordance with the Dhamma.
Hearing this, the king dispatched a minister named Kapila, who had mastered all the scriptures, and had a legal determination made regarding its status as something not spoken by the Buddha.

Having understood all this, he burned the Vetulla manuscripts and, having suppressed those wicked bhikkhus who had acquired them, he purified the Buddha’s dispensation (as recorded on page 12 of the *Nikāya-saṅgaha*). For it is said in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
“Having crushed the Vetulla doctrine and having carried out the suppression of the wicked...”
"And by the minister Kapila, he caused the teaching to shine.
Regarding the origin of the Sāgaliya sect:
furthermore, during the time of King Goṭhābhaya (797–810 BE), those inhabitants of Abhayagiri likewise [promoted] the Vetullavāda.

They showed themselves. At that time, however, a great elder named Ussiliyātissa, having heard of the refutation made against the Vetullavādin monks during the reign of King Vohārakatissa, thought: "This would have been appropriate at a time when the king was endowed with discernment; it is not good [now].
Thinking thus, he took about three hundred monks, saying, "We shall not be on one side with them."
Having gone to the Dakkhiṇagiri Monastery, he lived there as a separate sect from the Dhammaruci school.
Among them, a great elder named Sāgala, residing right there at Dakkhiṇagiri, gave expositions on the Āgamas.
From that time forth, the disciples of that elder were known as the Sāgaliyas. Their doctrine, too, [flourished] later during the reign of King Mahāsena.
It is spread out on page 13 of the *Nikāya* in the Jetavana Monastery.

Furthermore, King Goṭhābhaya [suppressed] the second refutation of the Vetullavāda in the five great monasteries known as the Mahāvihāra, the Cetiya, the Thūpārāma, the Issarasamaṇaka, and the Vessagiri-vihāra.
Having convened the great community of bhikkhus together in the monasteries and inquired about the situation, he realized that the Vetullavāda was not spoken by the Buddha.
Consequently, he branded sixty wicked bhikkhus who adhered to that doctrine with the mark of a dog and banished them from the kingdom.
He then burned the Vetulla manuscripts and purified the Buddha’s dispensation, as recorded in the verses at Mahāvaṃsa 36, 111–112, and on page 13 of the Nikāya.
At that time, among those monks who had been expelled from the kingdom, some went to the port city of Kāvīrapaṭṭana and resided there.
On that occasion, a young brahmin follower of another sect came to Kāvīra from another country;
seeing the offerings presented to those monks by the inhabitants of the port town, he was moved by their gain and honor, and he went forth into homelessness in their presence.
He became well known by the name Saṅghamitta. Having learned, through the legal deliberations of the Mahāvihāravāsins,
that those monks had been expelled from the kingdom by King Goṭhābhaya on account of their Vetullavāda views,
he became enraged at the Mahāvihāravāsins and thought, "I shall either cause them to adopt the Vetullavāda, or I shall uproot and destroy their monastery."
Thinking, "Having gone to the island of Siṃhala and won over the king, I shall teach the two sons of that king their craft," he began his efforts.
Nevertheless, setting aside the elder son, Jeṭṭhatissa— who was capable of understanding his own doctrine—
he took only the younger prince, Mahāsena, whom he could later persuade to act according to his word, and taught him the craft.
After the death of Vītiṇṇa, when Prince Jeṭṭhatissa ascended the throne (810–819 BE), he, fearing that king,
went to the port city of Kāvīra (as recorded in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, chapter 36, verse 113, etc., and in volume 14 of the *Nikāya-saṅgraha*). However,
during the time of King Mahāsena (819–845 BE), he returned once more to the island of Siṃhala and [resided] at the Abhayagiri Monastery.
Vasanta made various efforts to induce the Mahāvihāravāsins to adopt the Vetullavāda;
yet, being unable to make them accept it, he approached the king and, having persuaded him through various arguments, issued a royal decree stating:
"Whoever should give food to even a single monk dwelling in the Mahāvihāra shall be punished with a fine of one hundred [pieces of gold]."
He had a drum beaten throughout the city. At that time, the residents of the Mahāvihāra, while wandering for alms in the city, failed to obtain any food for three days.

They assembled at the Great Palace and said: "If, out of hunger, we were to accept what is unrighteous as righteous, many people would follow our example and fall into the states of misery, and we ourselves would all become guilty of an offense."
"Therefore, we shall not accept the Vetullavāda even for the sake of our lives.
Having thus deliberated, they abandoned all the monasteries, such as the Mahāvihāra and others, and went to the Rohaṇa country and the Malaya region (Mahāvaṃsa 37, verses 2–6;
Nikāyasaṅgaha, p. 14).
What is the Vetullavāda?
What indeed is this so-called Vetullavāda, because of which the residents of the Mahāvihāra felt such extreme loathing?
It is not possible now to explain the true nature of the Vetullavāda in every respect, whether by way of the books known by the name "Vetulla" or by way of the Nikāya itself.
This is because they are not well-known at present. However, in the *Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā* within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, several Vetullavāda positions are recorded, beginning at sections 793–794.

How so? — (1) “In the ultimate sense, the Saṅgha is nothing other than the paths and fruits; there is no Saṅgha apart from the paths and fruits. Furthermore, the paths and fruits do not receive anything; therefore, it should not be said that ‘the Saṅgha receives offerings. (1)
(2) "The Saṅgha is indeed the paths and fruits, yet they are not able to purify offerings; therefore, it should not be said that 'the Saṅgha purifies offerings.
(3) "The Saṅgha is indeed the paths and fruits, yet they do not consume anything; therefore, it should not be said that 'the Saṅgha eats, drinks, chews, or tastes.
"The Saṅgha is indeed the paths and fruits, yet it is impossible to give anything to them, nor can they receive anything."
(4) Nor does any benefit accrue to them through that gift; therefore, it should not be said that "what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit.

(5) Furthermore, the Buddha, the Blessed One, does not consume anything at all; however, for the sake of conforming to worldly custom, he displays himself as if he were consuming. Therefore, because there is no benefit [to him], it should not be said that "what is given to him is of great fruit.
(6) Moreover, the Blessed One was reborn in the Tusita heaven and dwells right there; he does not come to the human world, but merely displays a manifested form here.

(7) “The Blessed One, while staying in the Tusita heaven, dispatched an emanation for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. It was by that [emanation], and after receiving his teaching, that the Venerable Ānanda taught the Dhamma, not the Buddha, the Blessed One.
“One may engage in sexual intercourse with a single intention. Herein, this is the meaning:

‘with a single intention’ means either with a single intention of compassion, or with the intention, ‘May we be together in saṃsāra,’ [performing] acts such as worship of the Buddha together with a woman.”

"By making a resolution, there would be a single intention; thus, with such a single intention shared by both people, sexual intercourse may be practiced"—in this way the tenets of the Vetullavādins are handed down.
Only so many of their doctrines are now known from the perspective of the Theravāda texts.
And herein, by the first four doctrines, the Saṅgha as presented in the Suttantas is wrongly grasped, and the Saṅgha as presented in the Vinaya is rejected in every respect.
Following those, three doctrines are followers of the theory of creation by a Supreme Lord (issaranimmāna).
However, the nature of the final doctrine as a teaching contrary to the true Dhamma (asaddhamma) is exceedingly evident.
In the *Abhidhammasamuccaya*, however, the status of the Vetullaka Piṭaka as the Bodhisattva Piṭaka is elucidated;

therefore, even the doctrine found in the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, such as the *Saddhammapuṇḍarīka-sutta* and others, should be understood as the "Vetullaka doctrine" according to page 79 of the *Abhidhammasamuccaya*. [This concludes] the section on the destruction of the Mahāvihāra.
When the Mahāvihāravāsins had departed, abandoning all the monasteries in the manner previously described, the wicked monk Saṅghamitta persuaded the king;

he then caused the sixty-four additional pariveṇas and palaces, numbering three hundred in total, such as the Lohapāsāda, to be destroyed and uprooted from their foundations, and had them transported to the Abhayagiri Monastery.
Furthermore, having had the site of the monastery ploughed, [he established] another [monastery]...
He had it consecrated. Thus, at that time, the Mahāvihāra remained empty of monks for nine years, devoid of its inhabitants.

Then the King, through the words of his minister named Meghavaṇṇābhaya—who had become his virtuous friend—preceded by a stern rebuke, restored the Mahāvihāra to its former state and brought back those monks who had departed, [providing] with the four...
It was established by conditions in verses 37–30 of the *Mahāvaṃsa*, and on pages 14–15 of the *Nikāyasaṅgaha*.
Regarding the origin of the Jetavanavāsin Nikāya:
furthermore, the king, having become devoted to the monk Tissa the Deceitful (*Kuhakatissa Thera*), who resided at Dakkhiṇārāma and possessed a crooked mind, for his sake...
Within the boundary of the Mahāvihāra, he began to have the Jetavana Vihāra constructed in the Jotivana garden.
Unable to stop him, the monks residing at the Mahāvihāra departed from there once again. At that time as well, the Mahāvihāra remained empty of monks for nine months.
However, by his own personal inclination, the king established the Jetavana Vihāra there.
Having had it made, he gave it to that fraudulent Elder Tissa.
There, monks from the Sāgaliya monastery on Dakkhiṇagiri came and resided.

Later, during the time of King Ambasāmavera Silākāla (1067–1080 CE), they became proponents of the Vetullavāda, as recorded in verses 32 and others of the thirty-seventh chapter of the *Mahāvaṃsa*, and on page 15 of the *Nikāyasaṅgaṇī*.

Thus, even before the time of the arrival of the Elder Buddhaghosa Thera to the Island of Siṃhala (965 BE), three schools had arisen that held doctrines opposed to the pure Theravāda of the Mahāvihāravāsins:
the Abhayagirivāsins (455 BE), the Sāgaliyas (797–810 BE), and the Jetavanavāsins (829–845 BE). Among these, it was only the Abhayagirivāsins...
In particular, these [sects] are both well-known and powerful.
For they accept the Piṭaka of the pure Theravāda, as well as the Piṭaka of the Dhammaruci sect included among the Vajjiputtakas, the Piṭaka of the Mahīśāsaka and other sects, and the Mahāyāna Piṭaka.
Among these, the fact that they accepted the Piṭaka of the Dhammaruci sect is indeed well known. As for the Piṭaka of the Mahīśāsaka and other sects...
Furthermore, the fact that [the Mahāyāna] was accepted should be understood from the account of the Elder Bhikkhu Phāyiya’s observation of the sequence of the journey,

as well as from the names such as the *Vaṇṇapiṭaka* and others rejected in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*); likewise, the fact that the *Mahāyānapiṭaka* was accepted is also to be understood in this way.
The Discourse on the Toil of the Path of Effort:
Indeed, by the monk named Phāhiyañña, in the year 956 of the Buddha’s era, the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya Piṭaka,
the Dīgha Āgama, the Saṃyutta Āgama, and the Sannipāta Piṭaka— translated into the Pāli language from the island of Ceylon— were [brought] by himself.
That he was brought from the Cīna kingdom along with [the texts] is shown in the account of his journey.
And all of that was obtained by him from the Abhayagiri monastery alone, because the residents of the Mahāvihāra did not possess the Piṭakas that had been honored and established there.

Furthermore, the *Vaṇṇapiṭaka* and other works rejected in the Aṭṭhakathā would likely have been found right there, since they were not accepted by the Mahāvihāravāsins. Likewise, regarding the monk Phāhiya...
"At the time when [the Master] was residing on the island of Siṃhala (954–956 BE), approximately three thousand bhikkhus dwelt in the Mahāvihāra;
they mastered only the Piṭaka of the Theravāda, not the Mahāyāna Piṭaka.
At the Abhayagirivihāra, approximately five thousand bhikkhus dwelt; they, however, mastered both Piṭakas—the Mahāyāna Piṭaka as well as the Theravāda Piṭaka."
And it was shown by that very monk Cīna.
Furthermore, since the inhabitants of Abhayagiri also studied the Mahāyāna Piṭaka,
there would certainly have existed in that monastery even those texts composed by Assaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, who were the preeminent teachers among the Mahāyānikas.
For that very reason, the Venerable Ācariya Buddhaghosa, as well as other elders of that time residing at the Mahāvihāra who were endowed with great learning,
would certainly have known their lineage and names. Furthermore, in the southern province of India,
near the sea, in the district of Guṇṭha, there was a place called Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, where Nāgārjuna served as the preeminent teacher of the Mahāyānists.
Vasanta established [the work] in the Buddha’s dispensation.
Furthermore, there are signs indicating that the teacher Buddhaghosa was a native of that country, which will appear later (on page 33).
Therefore, it can be inferred that the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa must certainly have known both the method and the names of Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa.
Furthermore, the reason why the system or the name of those [masters] was not explained by him in his own commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*),
even though he knew them, is precisely because they belonged to other schools (*nikāyantara*). For instance, among those two— Assaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna—

Assaghoṣa (who lived within the period of 570–670 years after the Buddha’s parinibbāna) was included in the Sarvāstivāda school among the eleven sects that had branched off from the Theravāda, while Nāgārjuna...
He belongs to the Mahāyāna school that arose from groups such as the Mahāsaṅghika-Cetiyavādins;

furthermore, the Mahāvihāravāsins, from the very beginning, have preserved their own Piṭaka with great care in order to keep it unmixed with the doctrines of other schools, and this teacher Buddhaghosa was one of them. For it is said in the conclusions of his works:

“By one who was an ornament to the lineage of the Mahāvihāravāsins. Therefore, it should be understood that the teacher Buddhaghosa, though knowing their method, did not reveal it in his own works for the sake of avoiding confusion with the doctrines of other Nikāyas.
And up to this point, regarding the statement from the *Mahāvaṃsa* beginning with, “Born as a young Brahmin near the seat of enlightenment,” etc., [the connection is established].
The words of censure spoken by Dhammānanda Kosambī against Ācariya Buddhaghosa were examined through the process of critical investigation and found to be baseless.
Nevertheless, apart from that statement in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, no firm evidence is seen to establish the point that "Ācariya Buddhaghosa was born near the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa)."
Furthermore, even that which was stated in the *Buddhaghosuppatti* does not constitute a firm reason, because those words were spoken based solely upon the *Mahāvaṃsa*.
This concludes the discussion on the status of being a native of the kingdom of Burma.
However, some from the Maramma country say, "The teacher Buddhaghosa went from the city named Sathu in the Maramma country to the island of Ceylon and composed the commentaries on the Saṅgaha.
