"Born in Telaṅga"—many people born in Telaṅga went to and reside in the kingdom of Burma (Maramma) and the kingdom of Indochina;
from whence did this designation arise? It arose precisely from that word "Telaṅga. Likewise, it is said:
"Buddhaghosa, having composed the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), went from the island of Sri Lanka to the kingdom of Burma and resided right there in its western region."
"It is possible to preserve it, for its texts are more securely guarded in the kingdom of Burma than even in the kingdom of Ceylon," he said,
and thus it was established.
This is the reasoning regarding its origin in the kingdom of South India.
However, many modern discerning scholars, such as Dhammānanda and others, state that "the Venerable Ācariya Buddhaghosa was a native of the Dakkhiṇa-India country.
This, however, is the reasoning here: for the majority of the elders who were commentators on the *Aṭṭhakathās* and their sub-commentaries (*Ṭīkās*) were indeed natives of the Dakkhiṇa-India country.
For instance, [this is evident] from the *Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Abhidhammāvatāra-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Vinayavinicchaya-aṭṭhakathā*.
And the author [of the *Paramatthavinicchaya*] was the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta,

who was born in the city of Uragapura on the river Tambapaṇṇī in the kingdom of Coḷa and was a contemporary of the Elder Ācariya Buddhaghosa. As for the author of the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*,
and the *Paramatthavinicchaya*, some say that the author of the *Paramatthavinicchaya* was one person [different from the others].

Also, the teacher Dhammapāla Thera, a native of Kañcipura in the kingdom of Dakkhiṇa-indiya, was the author of the *Paramatthadīpanī*, which is a commentary on the *Udāna* and other texts included in the *Khuddakanikāya*. This [author] is likewise the same.
It should be understood. For it is said in the conclusion of the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the commentary on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*:
“Requested by the Elder Sumati, the Venerable Jotipāla;
while formerly dwelling together with me in Kañcīpura and other places.”
And here, "Kañcipura" refers to the very city now known as Kañjīvar, located approximately forty-five *mīla*s to the south-southwest of Madurā.
Likewise, in the conclusion of the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, it says:
"Requested by the wise Elder Buddhamitta..."
It is said: “Formerly, O messenger peacock, while living together in the city of Mayūrapaṭṭana.
Regarding this, those who seek out ancient traditions state that the place called Mayūradūtapura is the location currently known as Milapora near the city of Madarasā.
However, by these concluding verses, he makes it clear that he formerly resided in the kingdom of Dakkhiṇa India itself, near the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa).

Therefore, it cannot be denied that the teacher Buddhaghosa was a native of the southern Indian province (Dakkhiṇaindiyaraṭṭhika).

furthermore, Master Buddhaghosa thoroughly understands both what was spoken with reference to the Andhaka-ṭīkā and the manner in which its text was arranged in that country;

he is to be called "Moraṇḍakheṭaka," or "one who should be called Moraṇḍakheṭaka. Having thus established the meaning of the word as "by the one who should be called Moraṇḍakheṭaka," the sense should be understood as:

Regarding these three statements— that "the teacher Buddhaghosa was born near the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa)," "he was a native of the Maramma kingdom," and "he was a native of the Dakkhiṇa-indiya kingdom"—
the last one alone is the most authoritative, as it relies upon the word of the teacher himself.
Therefore, based on that very source, the origin of the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa should be understood in this way.
The Background Story of the Venerable Ācariya Buddhaghosa:
The Master Buddhaghosa was born in the village of Moraṇḍa in the kingdom of Dakkhiṇa India into a brahmin family during the tenth century of the Buddha’s era (901–1000 BE).
He had mastered the three Vedas as well as all the treatises on the various branches of knowledge and the arts.

Having sacrificed for the sake of the Buddha’s teaching and having heard the Dhamma, desiring to master it as well, he received both the going-forth and full ordination in that very same Theravāda monastery in the kingdom of Dakkhiṇa India from the monks headed by the Elder Revata, who were residents of the Mahāvihāra;
there he mastered the Pāḷi of the Tipiṭaka. While he was thus mastering the Pāḷi of the Tipiṭaka—
He realized: "This is the one-way path for the purification of vision and for the realization of Nibbāna.

And his teachers and preceptors, having recognized that he was endowed with the power of distinguished knowledge and perceiving that "the fame of this man’s reputation in the Buddha’s teaching will spread like that of the Buddha," gave him the name "Buddhaghosa" (Voice of the Buddha). Thus it is said:
“By one who has received the name Buddhaghosa from his teachers.

Having thus mastered the Pāli of the Three Piṭakas, while residing in Mayūradūtapattana—which is situated near the city of Madarasa—and in Kañcipura and other places, he gained familiarity with the Andhaka commentaries; yet, dissatisfied with them, he...
Desiring to gain proficiency in the Sinhalese commentaries and wishing to bring them up to date by translating them into the Pali language, he went to the island of Sri Lanka.
At that time, a king named Mahānāma was ruling over the island of Sri Lanka;
that king was devoted to the residents of the Abhayagiri monastery and supported them in particular.
However, some modern discerning scholars say this:
"Master Buddhaghosa must have lived even earlier than the time of King Sirimeghavaṇṇa (846 BE), due to his arrival in the Island of Siṃhala.
Their reason for this is that during the ninth year of that king's reign (855 BE), the Buddha’s tooth relic was brought from Kaliṅga Province to the Island of Siṃhala.
From that time forth, the Sinhalese kings have held a great festival for the worship of the relics every year.
And if the teacher Buddhaghosa had come to the island of Sri Lanka after that,
he too would have seen that magnificent festival and described it in his own books, just as Phāhiya did in his work concerning the time of King Mahānāma.
Having seen that [passage], he disclosed it in his own *Addhānakkama-kathā*, yet no such disclosure is found in the works of his teacher;

therefore, it is known that "the teacher Buddhaghosa came to the Island of Siṃhala even earlier than the time when the Tooth Relic was obtained and composed the commentaries. However, that is not a firm reason.
Indeed, in the commentary on the meaning of the Tipiṭaka Pāḷi, there is nothing whatsoever that must be disclosed as having been personally witnessed by oneself;
nor is the commentary on the meaning like a narrative of travels.

Furthermore, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, certain matters have been introduced and explained from the *Dīpavaṃsa*, and in the *Dīpavaṃsa*, [the account extends] up to the time of King Mahāsena.
(819–845-bu-va) Since the "occurrence" (*pavatti*) is explained [in the *Dīpavaṃsa*],
the *Dīpavaṃsa* itself could not have been written prior to the time of King Sirimeghavaṇṇa (845–873-bu-va). Furthermore, if the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) had been composed even earlier than that,
how could the *Dīpavaṃsa* possibly have been explained therein?

However, when Ācariya Buddhaghosa arrived at the Island of Siṃhala, he went specifically to the Mahāvihāra and there listened to the Siṃhalese commentaries from the great Siṃhalese Theras. For it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
“The Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*), the Great Sub-commentary (*Mahā-paccarī*), and the *Kurundi*—these are the three Siṃhalese commentaries.”
"Having heard [it] in the presence of the Elder, who was renowned by the name Buddhamitta, illustrious, wise, and an expert in the Vinaya"— thus ends the eighth [chapter], the concluding discourse.
By this statement from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is shown that only the three commentaries, beginning with the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, were actually heard.
[The explanation] has been shown. However, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the exposition of both the *Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā* has indeed been shown.
Why, then, did the Master not hear them from the Sīhaḷa Theras?
Regarding that, it is well known that the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā* was not heard [by him] because of its being a work of the Andhaka country and because he had already completed his study of it.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* (the Short Commentary) was not heard [by the author], because it is merely an abridgment of the *Mahāpaccarī-ṭṭhakathā*.

For instance, in the *Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā*, in the commentary on the introduction to the text (*ganthārambhavaṇṇanā*), it is stated in the commentary on the discourse regarding the commencement of the work (*ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā*) that even the *Cūḷapaccarī-ṭṭhakathā* and the *Andhaka-ṭṭhakathā* are included by the word "etc. (*ādi*). This is also mentioned in the *Sāratthadīpanī* and *Vimativinodanī* commentaries.

In the *Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā* (1.92), in the section on the *Pācittiya-khaṇḍa*, it is stated that the commentary on the introductory discourse (*ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā*) of the *Vinaya-vinicchaya-ṭīkā* was compiled from the *Andhaka-saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, the name "Cūḷapaccarī" does not appear anywhere in the *Samantapāsādikā*;
rather, only these names—*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, *Mahāpaccarī*, *Kurundi*, and *Andhaka-saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā*—are found there.
In many places, such as in Pārāyaṇa-vaṇṇanā 1.94, where it says, "But in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* and in the *Mahāpaccarī*," the same interpretation is shown for both.
Therefore, the commentary stated in the *Vajirabuddhi* as the *Cūḷapaccarī* must be a commentary composed in brief by extracting [material] from the *Mahāpaccarī*; and that...
Because it was composed in brief, it came to be known as the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* (the Short Commentary).
This being the case, since the *Mahāpaccarī* was heard by [Buddhaghosa], that too would be considered "heard"; thus, it should not be understood that he heard it from his teacher.

In this way, even as he was hearing the Sinhalese commentaries, Master Buddhaghosa’s possession of the excellence of the power of his sharp, profound, and swift intuitive knowledge (*javana-ñāṇa*) became manifest.
Having recognized his state of being endowed with a multitude of qualities such as moral virtue, conduct, speed, and gentleness, adorned by supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy;
his possession of the proficiency of insight capable of plunging into the depths of both his own and other systems of tenets;
and his mastery of the methods of exposition praised in numerous scriptural traditions—at the conclusion of the task of listening to him—
The elders, beginning with Saṅghapāla, each individually requested him to compose the Visuddhimagga and other such treatises.
Furthermore, the Master’s possession of the aforementioned qualities is evident from his own words. For it is said in the conclusions of his own compositions:—

“Adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a collection of virtues such as virtue, conduct, gentleness, and humility; and possessed of analytical discernment capable of plunging into the depths of both our own system and those of other systems,” and so forth.

In this context, by the phrase “capable of plunging into the depths of both our own system and those of other systems,” it is indicated that the Venerable Teacher Buddhaghosa was proficient in his own system—the method of teaching known as the *Visuddhika-Theravāda* of the Mahāvihāravāsins—and also in all other systems, from the Mahāsaṅghikas up to the Mahāyānists.
He was skilled in the systems of other schools— namely, the doctrines found in the various scriptural collections (*piṭaka*) of others known as "other traditions" (*parasamaya*)—
as well as in the systems of contemporary non-Buddhist ascetics and brahmins known as the "three Vedas" and so forth;
and he was capable of penetrating even the dense thickets of those very traditions, both his own and others', which consist of meanings that are difficult to fathom and difficult to understand.

"He is capable" is what he demonstrates. By the phrase "endowed with discernment," it should be understood that the Elder Master Buddhaghosa demonstrates that he is capable of both condensing and reorganizing the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
[This concludes] the reason for the request.
But why did they request that from him? It is said:

for the Mahāvihāravāsins, from the very beginning, have both learned and taught only the ancient Piṭaka-pāḷi exactly as it was chanted in the three councils (*saṅgītis*) in the Pāḷi language, and exactly as it was committed to books during the time of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi (455–467 CE). They do not [teach] otherwise.
The Piṭaka was established by Sakkatāra. And the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) were composed approximately three hundred years prior [to that].

For indeed, in the commentaries, no account of the Sihaḷika Theras or others is seen after the time of King Vasabha (609–653 CE), with the exception of the account of King Mahāsena (Aṭṭhasālinī 2.236–237), up until the time of Ācariya Buddhaghosa.
Furthermore, those very same ancient commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) exist [there] without having been newly composed.
Consequently, for the most part, people have neither developed a desire nor a resolve to become familiar with their Piṭakas.

Moreover, they are unable to propagate their own Piṭakas in other islands because the commentaries were composed in the language of the Island (Sinhala). This refers to the residents of the Abhayagiri monastery.
However, since the time of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī, people have been constantly acquiring and teaching the Dhammaruci Nikāya Piṭaka and the Mahāyāna Piṭaka,
which were composed in the Pāli language; consequently, most people have developed a desire and an enthusiasm for becoming familiar with these Piṭakas, [seeking] nothing but what is ever new.
For beings indeed hold their own [views] dear. It is precisely for this reason that they are able to propagate their own doctrines even on other islands.

Therefore, those elders residing at the Mahāvihāra, desiring to compose their own Sinhalese commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) in the Pāli language, recognized the specific power of the knowledge of the Venerable Ācariya Buddhaghosa and his possession of the aforementioned qualities, as he was capable of performing such a task.
It should be understood that having understood this, they made their request.
Regarding the composition of the *Visuddhimagga*:
first, the teacher Buddhaghosa, having been requested by the Elder Saṅghapāla, [composed] the *Visuddhimagga* for the Mahāvihāra.
In the southern part of the city, in the palace of the lord of the great town, [the author] resided and composed this *Visuddhimagga*.
By this much, the meaning of these questions—“But by whom was this *Visuddhimagga* made? When was it made?
Where was it made? And why was it made?”—has been explained in detail.

Now we shall explain the meaning of the questions beginning with "For what purpose was it composed? Among these, the meaning of the question "For what purpose was it composed? has already been explained by the Teacher himself.

How so? "Having obtained the going-forth in the Conqueror’s dispensation, which is so very difficult to find, [he practiced] the secure collection of virtue and the like, the straight path for purification."
Those who do not know things as they truly are, even if they desire purity here in this world,
do not attain purification despite their striving, O practitioners of yoga. For them,
this [work] is a source of joy, providing a most thorough and clear determination.
“I shall speak the *Visuddhimagga*, which is based on the method of teaching of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
As I speak it with diligence, may all you virtuous ones who desire purification listen attentively. (Visuddhi 1.2)

Therefore, this *Visuddhimagga* (Path of Purification) should be understood as having been composed for the sake of noble people who desire Nibbāna—known as purification—in order that they may know, as it truly is, the path of purification consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom; this is its primary purpose.
However, in terms of secondary purposes, it was also intended so that the texts might be made more concise than in the commentaries on the four Āgamas.
It should be understood as "which one. For it is said in the commentaries on the Āgamas:
"This Path of Purification stands in the midst of all four Āgamas and will clarify the meaning therein exactly as it was spoken."
"Thus indeed was it done by me"—this is the end of the introductory discourse on the composition of the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the question "On what basis was it composed?", the meaning of this has also been explained by the Teacher himself. For it is said here at the beginning of the work: [text follows]
“Purity is that which is based on the method of teaching of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
1.2. Likewise, in the conclusion:
“The exposition of the meanings of those categories beginning with virtue;”
"Having collected almost all of that which is stated according to the method of the commentaries of the five Nikāyas,
and having explained it free from almost all faults of confusion,
[this work] has been made manifest. — Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā, Introduction to the Book (Ganthārambhakathā).
By this statement, however, this meaning becomes clear:

“The Master, while composing the *Visuddhimagga*, drew upon the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) of the five Nikāyas—known as the method of teaching of the Mahāvihāravāsins—and compiled all the analytical explanations (*vinicchaya*) stated therein.
Therefore, whatever word-commentary or analytical explanation occurs here...

Whatever is shown here, whether it be the subject matter or the means of accomplishment, all of that should be understood as having been brought from the ancient Sinhala *Aṭṭhakathā*—which consists of commentaries on the various specific words of the established Canon—and presented solely by way of linguistic translation.
For this *Visuddhimagga* was not composed merely through the power of his own knowledge, nor was it intended merely as an independent treatise; [rather, it is a systematic compilation].
Rather, it was composed as a constituent part of all four *Āgama* commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*). For it is stated in their conclusion:
"Since the *Visuddhimagga*, consisting of fifty-nine recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*), was composed for the purpose of elucidating the meaning of the *Āgamas*,"

"Therefore, together with that companion, according to the count of recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) in the commentary, it is precisely measured and delimited as one hundred and forty [sections]," and so forth—this is the concluding discourse from the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*, section 3.

Furthermore, in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the exposition on the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*), it says: "This, first of all, is in the discourse on purification..."
The method [is as follows]. In the *Ariyavaṃsa-kathā*, however, two discourses beginning with “...and so forth” have been stated;

it should be understood that these too are included within the teaching-method (*desanā-naya*) of the Mahāvihāravāsins and are indeed the very supports for this *Visuddhimagga*. The manner of performing that [method] is as follows:
"In what manner was it made?"—here, it was made in the very same manner as stated in the immediately preceding question. For thus the Teacher [said] from the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*:
"A wise man, established in virtue, developing the mind and wisdom, ardent and prudent, that bhikkhu shall disentangle this tangle" (*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.23).
Having first presented this verse, he analyzed in detail each of the virtues, concentrations, and wisdoms mentioned therein according to their specific applications. While doing so,
he extracted from all five Nikāyas the sūtra passages associated with virtue, concentration, and wisdom,
and demonstrated their meaning by translating them from the Sinhalese commentaries.
He explained the Sīhaḷika sources mentioned therein, as well as their detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*).

In particular, at that time, he pointed out numerous instances where views contrary to his own school and those of other schools were prevalent, and he refuted them with logical reasoning. How so? For instance, in the *Cariyāvaṇṇanā*, it says:
"In that regard, first, the three preceding temperaments have their origins in past habits and the humors of the physical elements (*dhātu-dosa*)."

So some say. It is said that one who was previously abundant in the performance of desirable and wholesome deeds is of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*); or one who has fallen from a heavenly realm and is reborn here.
One who was previously abundant in acts of cutting, killing, binding, and enmity is of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*);
or one who has fallen from the hells or the womb of a *nāga* and is reborn here. One who was previously abundant in drinking intoxicants and devoid of study and inquiry...
They say that the origins of past conduct are as follows: one is of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*) because one has passed away from the animal realm and been reborn here;
or, due to the predominance of two elements, a person is of deluded temperament—namely, the earth element and the water element;
due to the predominance of the other two, one is of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*); and when all are equal, one is of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*).

"Furthermore, one with an excess of phlegm (*semha*) is of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*); one with an excess of wind (*vāta*) is of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*). Or, one with an excess of phlegm is of deluded temperament; one with an excess of wind is of lustful temperament.
Thus they speak of the causes based on the humors (*dhātu-dosa-nidāna*). Having shown this single opinion, he [continues]:
"In that regard, because even those who previously performed much desirable application and beautiful karma, having passed away from heaven, have been reborn here..."

"Not all are of a lustful temperament (rāgacarita), nor are the others of a hateful or deluded temperament (dosamohacarita). Likewise, there is no fixed rule regarding the predominance of the elements (dhātu) according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, in the section on the predominance of hatred, only the pair of lust and delusion are mentioned, and that too is internally contradictory.
Therefore, all of this is an indeterminate statement"—thus [the author of] the *Visuddhimagga* rejects [this position]. 1.44.
This is described in the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā*, titled *Paramatthamañjūsā*, in the passage beginning: “‘A certain one’ refers to the Elder Upatissa;
for it was stated thus in the *Vimuttimagga*,” and so forth (*Visuddhi-ṭī.* 1.44).
[This concludes] the section on the *Vimuttimagga*.

What is this so-called Path to Liberation (*vimuttimagga*)? It is a manual of practice that, like the *Visuddhimagga*, elucidates virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*paññā*) by analyzing them individually. For therein it is said:
“Virtue, concentration, and wisdom, And unsurpassed liberation— These qualities were awakened to By the illustrious Gotama. (Dīgha Nikāya 2.186; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.1)

Having first presented this verse, the virtues of morality (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), and liberation (*vimutti*) were explained by means of a commentary on its meaning, each being analyzed individually.
That text was seen right here in the country of Cīna and translated into the Cīna language by a monk named Saṅghapāla. But by whom [was it brought], from where, and why there?
That he was brought here is not well known. However, Saṅghapāla’s teacher was a Mahāyāna monk named Guṇabhadra, a native of the Middle Country.
While traveling from the kingdom of Indiya to the kingdom of Cīna, he first went to the island of Siṃhala and from there proceeded to the kingdom of Cīna.
At that time, it was likely he who brought the *Vimuttimagga* and the *Visuddhimagga*.
For in that *Vimuttimagga*, the demonstration of the origins of former habits and the demonstration of the origins of the elements are presented exactly as they appear in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, in the demonstration of the origins of the defilements, it says: "One with an excess of phlegm is of lustful temperament;

one with an excess of bile is of hateful temperament; one with an excess of wind is of deluded temperament. Or, one with an excess of phlegm is of deluded temperament; one with an excess of wind is of lustful temperament."
A restriction to hatred alone has been stated for all three—greed, hatred, and delusion.

However, in the *Diṭṭhavimuttimaggapotthaka* by the teacher Buddhaghosa, the reading “one whose temperament is dominated by hatred is one in whom bile is predominant” (*pittādhiko dosacarito*) would be deficient.
Furthermore, many other [readings] rejected in the *Visuddhimagga* appear there in the *Vimuttimagga* as things that ought to be accepted. How so?

In the *Sīlaniddesa* (p. 8), the following meaning—which is rejected there by the statement, “But others explain the meaning here in such a manner as ‘the meaning of coolness is the meaning of virtue (*sīla*),’ ‘the meaning of being cool is the meaning of virtue,’ and so forth”—is nevertheless seen as something that should be accepted.
Likewise, in the *Dhutaṅganiddesa* (p. 78), regarding those for whom the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is excluded from the triad of wholesome states (*kusalattika*), it is said:

“For them, in terms of actual meaning, there is no such thing as an ascetic practice at all; since it does not exist, of what could there be the shaking off (*dhunana*) to constitute an ‘ascetic practice’ (*dhutaṅga*)? [This applies] to the qualities of shaking off (*dhutaguṇa*).”
Furthermore, it would entail a contradiction with the statement "he conducts himself having undertaken [the practice]," and therefore that [position] should not be accepted;
for even the *dhutaṅga* of formal prescription (*paññatti*) is seen there. However, in the *Mahāṭīkā* (1–104), it is commented:
"'Of those' refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri; for they say that what is called a *dhutaṅga* is a formal prescription."

Likewise, in the description of the earth-kasiṇa (1, 144), a certain opinion that is rejected there is seen, namely: "Some explain it thus: 'Purification of the way' refers to access together with its requisites;
'intensification of equanimity' refers to absorption; and 'gladdening' refers to reviewing.
However, in the *Mahāṭīkā* (1, 172), it is explained: "'Some' refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri."
Likewise, in the Exposition of the Aggregates (*Khandhaniddesa*, p.

80), after citing other types of material form—such as "material form of strength, material form of growth, material form of birth, material form of disease, and according to the opinion of some, material form of torpor"—the fact that these were rejected in the Ancient Commentary (*Porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) is made clear.
In the Great Commentary (*Mahāṭīkā*), it is explained: "'Of some' refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri."
Among those, birth-form (*jātirūpa*) and sleep-form (*middharūpa*) have been shown in the Path of Liberation (*Vimuttimagga*). It is not merely that they are shown;

rather, the actual existence of sleep-form has also been established by such statements as: "Sleep is threefold: born of nutriment (*āhāraja*), born of temperature (*utuja*), and born of mind (*cittaja*).
Among these, only that born of mind is an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*); however, the other two may exist even in an Arhat. And so forth.

From this much, it can be understood that the fact of the *Vimuttimagga* not having the same meaning as the *Visuddhimagga* was stated [by Buddhaghosa], and that the residents of Abhayagiri accepted that text.
Furthermore, many other such statements of disagreement are indeed found therein; however, it is not possible to show all of them here.

For the most part, however, its method of exposition is like that of the *Visuddhimagga*. Indeed, whatever text from the *Abhidhamma-vibhaṅga*, the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, or other suttas is brought forward and presented in the *Visuddhimagga* as a supporting authority, that very text is for the most part found there as well.
Having extracted a small portion of these, we shall present them here for the sake of inference.

The passage from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* cited in the *Visuddhimagga* (p. 47) as beginning, “The five precepts: the abandoning of killing is virtue,” and so forth, is indeed found in the *Vimuttimagga* as well.

Furthermore, the statement shown in the *Visuddhimagga* (p. 137) as being spoken in the *Peṭaka*—namely, “Concentration is the antidote to sensual desire... [and] sustained thought is the antidote to doubt”—is likewise presented there in that very same way.
"It is stated in the *Tipeṭaka*" is what has been pointed out. By "in the *Tipeṭaka*," it is likely meant with reference to both the name [of the work] and the *Peṭakopadesa* itself.

For therein, in the commentary on the reading "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*), it says: "Through the fulfillment of non-greed, seclusion from sensual pleasures is accomplished;
through the fulfillment of non-hatred... through the fulfillment of non-delusion, seclusion from unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) is accomplished."
The fact that this passage is stated in the *Ti-piṭaka* has been demonstrated. That passage is found in the *Peṭakopadesa* (page 262) as:
“Therein, for the fulfillment of non-greed, one is secluded from sensual pleasures,” and so forth.

And just as in the *Visuddhimagga* (page 1, 258), where the canonical text beginning with “This too, monks, is the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, when developed” is presented by being brought over from the *Mahāvagga-saṃyutta*, it is exactly the same there as well.

Just as in the *Visuddhimagga* (vol. 1, p. 272), the Pāli passage beginning with “For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the inhalation with mindfulness,” and so forth, as well as the Pāli passage on the simile of the saw (vol.
1, p. 273), have been brought from the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* and presented there;

it is exactly the same in that [work]. And just as in the *Visuddhimagga* (vol. 2, p. 69), the Pāli passage beginning with “What is wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayā paññā*)? and so forth... [is found] therein.

The textual passage beginning with "What is skill in acquisition? (Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga, p. 71) and the textual passage beginning with "Knowledge regarding suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning" have been brought forward and shown from the *Abhidhamma-vibhaṅga*; it is the same there as well.

Furthermore, all the explanations concerning the classifications of wisdom—such as the singlefold, twofold, and so forth—stated therein are for the most part identical to the explanations given in the *Visuddhimagga*.
“By means of that clarity of the eye by which one perceives forms, this is limited and subtle, comparable to the head of a louse”—this is purity. (Visuddhi 2.436;
Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā 596) — This verse is also shown as having been spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta Thera in the *Vimuttimagga*.
Furthermore, the term "like the head of a gnat" (*ūkāsirasamūpama*) is seen there; however, that may be merely a scribal error by successive copyists.

Regarding the four truths—which, as in the *Visuddhimagga*, are included [in this work] according to their verbal meaning, their characteristics, their completeness (neither deficient nor redundant), and their sequence—
The analysis has been shown both by way of classification and by way of similes; and that is for the most part identical with the *Visuddhimagga*.

Just as in the *Visuddhimagga* (II, 242–245), within the discussion on comprehension-knowledge (*sammasanañāṇa*), the method of comprehending the five aggregates individually—both by way of the elevenfold classification such as past and so forth, and by way of the three characteristics such as impermanence—is demonstrated, it is exactly the same there as well.

However, regarding the phenomena beginning with the eye and ending with aging-and-death, the method of comprehension by means of the three characteristics—impermanence and so forth—is shown there for exactly sixty phenomena, ending with the investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicāra*).
In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, in the description of purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi-niddesa*), it is stated: “The pair, name-and-form... [and so on]” (pp. 230–232).

The verse beginning with “Both conditions break apart,” the six verses beginning with “They do not arise from the eye,” and the six verses beginning with “They do not arise by their own power” are presented in the *Vimuttimagga* within the discourse on the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa*).
Only a very slight variation in the readings is observed among them.

In the *Visuddhimagga* (on pages 261–2), the method of comprehension by groups and by pairs regarding the seven immaterial beings is stated according to the system of the discourse on the Noble Lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*). This same method is shown in the *Vimuttimagga* within the discussion on the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇa*).

Furthermore, in the *Vimuttimagga*, in the commentary on the meaning of the term "knower of the world" (*lokavidū*) in the discourse on the recollection of the Buddha, only two worlds are shown—namely, the world of sentient beings and the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*)—and not the world of space (*okāsaloka*), as is the case in the *Visuddhimagga* (on pages 199–200).
To this extent, it is possible to infer what kind of text the *Vimuttimagga* is.
However, just as it is not a text of the Mahāvihāravāsins, so too it is certainly not a text of the Mahāyānikas, because it was composed based solely upon the Theravāda Piṭaka.
Furthermore, since there is not even a single name such as "Sīhaḷadīpika" (of the Island of Ceylon) or "Theravāda" mentioned therein...
It is not seen; therefore, it was not composed on the island of Siṃhala.
However, both the name and the terminology of the Indira kingdom appear in many places therein; therefore, it must have been composed in the Indira kingdom.
Furthermore, its dependence upon the *Peṭakopadesa* is seen in many places, and specifically regarding the nature of *middha* (drowsiness).
The existence [of the path] and the existence of that Arahant are shown by depending on that very [text].

Furthermore, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-gaṇṭhipada* and in the commentary on the word *peṭaka* (Peṭakopadesa) at Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā 1.1.36, it is described thus: "The *Peṭaka* is the commentary on the meaning of the Suttanta Piṭaka;
it is the manual of the Mahīśāsakas. Therefore, this *Vimuttimagga* was composed by one belonging to the Mahīśāsaka school.
"It was composed," such is our opinion. Furthermore,
the *Visuddhimagga*, which is an exposition of the commentary on the *Nissaya*,
was not composed solely in the manner previously described, but also in the manner that is now being stated.

For instance, the Elder Ācariya Buddhaghosa, having compiled from the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) and presenting them through a transformation of language, would—whenever any commentary on the meaning or analysis was subject to doubt—state:
"This is said in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā" (1, 263), or "It is said in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathās," or "But in the Majjhima-aṭṭhakathās... (1, ...).
"Or [it is] the reciters of the *Aṅguttara*," (1, 72); "or it is a determination according to the opinion of the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*)," (1, 99);
"and this has also been stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāsūti*)," (1, 118); "or that is rejected in the commentaries," (1, 134);
"or it is the opinion of the reciters of the *Dīgha* and the reciters of the *Saṃyutta*"; or "the reciters of the *Majjhima* accept it."
"Or" (vā) (1, 267); "in the commentaries it is called 'determination' (vinicchaya)," thus say the Dīgha-bhāṇakas first;
"but the Majjhima-bhāṇakas say" (1, 277); "in the Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā, however...
this sequence is stated, but it does not agree with the Pāḷi," thus say the Majjhima-bhāṇakas first; "but the Saṃyutta-bhāṇakas [say]" (2, 62).

Whether it was stated as "it is said in the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*" (2, 63) or "but in the *Aṭṭhakathā*" (2, 80), he thus revealed the sources for those various analyses of the commentary on the meaning;
and while dispelling the doubts arising in later generations, he presented them.
Therefore, at the time of composing this *Visuddhimagga*, all the Sinhalese commentaries were [available] in the presence of the Master.
The fact that these [teachings] exist, that they were previously heard by the Teacher from the Sīhaḷa Theras,
and that this *Visuddhimagga* was written by the Teacher after he had mastered everything that is to be grasped from them— this meaning becomes exceedingly clear.
Therefore, as it is said in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
The words beginning with “The Saṅgha gave you the power of these two verses” are spoken as a statement of praise,
with the intention that “the teacher Buddhaghosa composed the Visuddhimagga after looking at only those two verses and without consulting any other book. This should be understood as mere praise.
Regarding the citation of ancient sayings:
the Master did not merely present the *Aṭṭhakathā* as his sole source of reliance; rather, he also cited the words of the ancients, beginning with the phrase "But the ancients said.
This is seen here in twenty-two instances concerning purification (Visuddhi). 1.15.

Who, then, are these called "ancients"? They should be understood as those included among the compilers up until the time of the Fourth Council, or as great elders (*mahāthera*) of a similar standing. For it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (pp. 292–293):
"He wavers in regard to illumination and knowledge, and in regard to rapture... [and so on]."
“He is skilled in agitation regarding the Dhamma and does not fall into distraction”—
thus these verses, which have come down [in the pages numbered 273–4], are shown here as being the words of the ancients.
And if these verses had been inserted by the compilers of the Council, they would have appeared just as they do in the Parivāra-pāḷi (page 3).
The verses illustrating the lineage of teachers (*ācariyaparamparādīpikā gāthāyo*) are presented in the *Samantapāsādikā* (p. 46) as "ancient words" (*porāṇavacanabhāvena*).
This being the case, it should be understood that those very compilers of the Council (*saṅgītikārā*) are the "ancients.

Alternatively, if they were spoken by the teacher of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* himself, then the "ancients" would be the Great Elders (*mahātherā*) who, like him, are worthy of honor, trustworthy, and credible.

[This] should be understood. In the *Samantapāsādikā*, the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, and other works, in passages such as "But the ancients explain it thus," similar teachers are referred to as "the ancients" (*porāṇā*).
[This concludes] the composition of the Vinaya commentary.

The Master, however, having composed this treatise on the Path of Purification (*Visuddhimagga*) in the manner described above, subsequently composed other commentaries on the Three Pitakas in due order.

How so? At the request of the Elder Buddhasiri, he composed the Vinaya commentary named *Samantapāsādikā* in the meditation hall courtyard on the southern side of the Mahāvihāra, in the palace of the lord of the great city.
Vasanta composed it. This work was begun in the twentieth year of King Mahānāma—whose other name was Siripāla (973 BE)—and was brought to completion in his twenty-first year (974 BE).

While composing it, he took the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* (Great Commentary), which had been brought by the Elder Mahinda and was written in the Sinhalese language, as its body, and [supplemented it] with the *Mahāpaccarī*, *Kuruṇḍī*, *Saṅkhepa*, and *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*.

Having taken what was to be taken, he composed it by including the Theravāda—the formal adjudications of the ancient Mahātheras who were experts in the Vinaya—which had been well-known in the island of Siṃhala down to the time of King Vasabha. For this is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"And in undertaking that commentary, [he took] the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*) as its body."
"Having likewise consulted the Mahāpaccarī and those renowned as the Kurundi and others,
I shall properly undertake this commentary— a sub-commentary that contains the Theravāda—
even while not abandoning the reasoned meaning stated in the Aṭṭhakathās."
“The Great Monastery of the Teacher, adorned by the Great Bodhi Tree, stands established upon a plot of ground in the Mahāmegha Grove.
To its southern side is the supreme House of Exertion.”
It is frequented by the Saṅgha of monks who possess virtuous conduct.
Born of a noble family, he always attends upon the Saṅgha;
with unshakable faith, he is devoted to the Three Jewels.
There, the one known as Mahānigamasāmī had built a delightful palace, adorned with a beautiful perimeter wall;
it was endowed with trees providing abundant shade and possessed a reservoir of excellent water.
While residing there in the palace of the lord of the great city,
the commentary on the Vinaya was undertaken and successfully completed by one who had dedicated it to the Elder named Buddhasiri, whose conduct was pure and virtuous.
While King Siripālana— named after his protection of the entire island of Laṅkā,
free from all affliction, and who was the very abode of the glory of King Sirinivāsa—
was ruling, in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the Jayasaṃvacchara era, this [work]...
"Initiated in the twenty-first [year], it was completed when [that year] arrived.
In a world agitated by calamities, this [work]—being free from calamity—has reached its conclusion in just one year. Thus ends the eighth [chapter], the concluding discourse.
This *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya commentary, according to the edition of the Sixth Council recently printed,
consists of approximately three hundred and fifty-eight pages (1,358).
In comparison with its completion in a single year, [the previous version] consisted of approximately seven hundred and twenty-four pages.
(724) It can be known that even the *Visuddhimagga* must have been completed in at least five or six months.
Therefore, as for the statement of praise found in the *Buddhaghosuppatti*, based on the account in the *Mahāvaṃsa*,
which says, "The *Visuddhimagga* was written and completed by the teacher Buddhaghosa in a single night after writing it three times," that is merely the [subjective] opinion of its author.
It should be understood that this is merely a matter of praise.

But is it not the case that in this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), an extension (*atidesa*) to the traditional commentaries (*āgama-aṭṭhakathā*) is seen by means of qualifying names such as "Sumaṅgalavilāsinī" and so forth [in the passage] "Pārāyaṇa-aṭṭha"? How, then, is it to be understood that this [commentary] was composed earlier than those?
Because of the mutual cross-references in the Master’s commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*),

because of the supreme importance of the Vinaya Piṭaka, because of its particular esteem by the Mahāvihāravāsins, because it conforms to the sequence of the Councils (*saṅgīti*), because the introductory narrative (*nidānakathā*) is presented here in its entirety,
and because the method of composition is revealed at the conclusion by stating that he first heard the Sinhalese commentaries— excluding only the *Visuddhimagga*— [this work was composed].

It should be understood that this very [work] was composed first. In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, a reference is seen by way of its general name alone—such as "in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā," or "in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathās," or "in the Majjhima-aṭṭhakathās"—but not by way of its specific names such as the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Therefore, its status as being composed before all others is indeed evident. This reference here to the commentaries on the Āgamas is from the *Pārāyaṇa-aṭṭhakathā*.

1.15 "In this [work] also, there [is]... (Dīghanikāya Aṭṭhakathā, vol. 1, p. 8). Thus, the extension of application (*atidesa*) from one to another can be accomplished either by way of the teacher’s mind having well-established it, or by completing [the work] without a sequence of first and last. How so?
For while the Teacher was completely finishing the *Visuddhimagga* and composing each individual commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), such as the *Samantapāsādikā*, etc., [he did so].
Wherever a detailed commentary on the meaning ought to be set forth in other commentaries,
having first mentally determined and established it with the thought, "I shall explain this in such-and-such a place," and having referred to it by way of cross-reference,
then when reaching the place thus determined, those [explanations] would be provided in detail by one who speaks. For each and every one...

Or, at the time when completion is nearly reached, having set aside that [first] and performed this and that [subsequent action] in such a way, all of them would be brought to final conclusion neither before nor after one another;
thus it should be understood that, by way of either of these two modes, there is a mutual extension (*atidesa*) of the Teacher’s commentary.

As for the composition of the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, the Master composed it at the request of the Elder Dāṭhānāga, a resident of the Sumaṅgala Monastery. Indeed, this is stated in its conclusion:
“Requested by the one of steadfast virtue who dwells in the Sumaṅgala Monastery...”
By the Elder Dāṭhānāga, a successor in the lineage of the Elders,
this commentary on the *Dīgha Āgama*— which elucidates the multitude of qualities of the One Possessing the Ten Powers—
was undertaken under the name *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*.
"For this has been completed by taking the essence from the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*). This is the concluding discourse of the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*.

The commentary on the *Majjhimanikāya* named *Papañcasūdanī* was composed at the request of the Venerable Buddhamitta Thera, who was formerly residing with [the author] in the city of Mayūradūta. Indeed, it is stated in its conclusion:
"At the request of the wise Elder, the Venerable Buddhamitta..."
Formerly, while residing together at the monastery of Mayūradūtapatta,
I have begun to compose this sub-commentary, the *Papañcasūdani*, upon the *Majjhimanikāya-ṭṭhakathā*,
the best of the Majjhima Nikāya commentaries, which destroys the arguments of opponents.
"For this has been completed by taking the essence from the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā). This is the concluding discourse of the *Aṭṭhaka-nipāta* of the *Maṇisāra*.
The commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, named *Sāratthappakāsinī*, was composed at the request of the venerable Elder Jotipāla. Indeed, it is stated in its conclusion:
"For the purpose of composing this, by the Elder, the venerable Jotipāla..."

“By the merit that was attained by me— Sucisīla, who, desiring the prosperity of the Dispensation and possessing beautiful virtues, requested me while making manifest his knowledge of well-spoken words—
by that merit may all people become happy. (Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 3.5, Concluding Statement)
The Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttaranikāya, was requested by the Venerable Jotipāla Thera while he was residing together with [the author] in the Dakkhiṇa-Indiya kingdom,
in Kañcipura and other places, as well as in the Mahāvihāra on the island of Siṃhala;
likewise, it was requested by the lay follower Jīvaka, who had mastered the Tipiṭaka, remaining as unshakable in his nature as a tree struck by the wind.
Having been requested by Sumati, who was established in the immovable True Dhamma and lived a pure livelihood, he performed it. For this is said in its conclusion:
“Requested by the Elder Sumati, the venerable Jotipāla;
By me, while previously living together in Kañcipurī and other places.”
While residing at the Mahāvihāra on the island of Tambapaṇṇi,
even though the True Dhamma remained unshaken— like a tree unmoved when struck by the wind—
the one of excellent wisdom, having reached the further shore of the ocean of the Three Piṭakas, stood firm.
He was entreated by the physician Jīvaka with a livelihood of complete purity;
he who was skilled in the delivery of Dhamma discourses, surrounded by immeasurable preachers of the Dhamma,
and who delighted in and practiced his own manifold system.
Desiring the long endurance of the noble dispensation,
I have begun to compose this commentary on the *Aṅguttara-nikāya*.
Having extracted the essence from the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*), this work has now been completed.

"Since my desire to provide a commentary on the entire Āgama—measuring ninety-four [vaggas] in recitation sections (bhāṇavāra)—has been fulfilled by this work, it shall therefore have the name *Manorathapūraṇī* ('The Fulfilled Desire').
This is the concluding discourse from the *Aṅguttara Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*. 3.11. Nigamanakathā.
Furthermore, while composing these four commentaries on the Āgamas, the teacher Buddhaghosa produced them by means of translating the language of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*—
known as the *Mūla-aṭṭhakathā*— which had been brought by the Elder Mahāmahinda, and by way of condensing the extensive discursive methods that recur repeatedly therein.
For this is stated at the beginning of the work:
“However, by the great Mahinda, who had arrived in the island of Siṃhala through his power,
these [teachings] were established in the Siṃhala language for the benefit of the island-dwellers.
Having now set aside that delightful Siṃhala language, I [shall speak] in [this] language;”
“Laying out that which is appropriate for the method of the Discourses (Tantinayā), free from fault...
[and so on] ...having abandoned the meaning that has come again and again, I shall clarify the true meaning.
Likewise, in the conclusion as well:
“Indeed, this has been completed by taking the essence from the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā),” says the concluding statement of the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*;
and also, “By me, while composing this, having taken the essence of the Root Commentary (Mūla-aṭṭhakathā),” says the concluding statement of the *Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, in the body of the text itself, as in the *Samantapāsādikā*, there are references such as “in the Mahāpaccarī” and “in the Kurundi.”
No exposition detailing the different classifications of the *vinicchaya* (analytical summaries) is found there, nor likewise in the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathās*.

From this it is known that, among the Sutta and Abhidhamma commentaries, there were no ancient Sinhalese commentaries named the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Mahā-paccarī*, and so forth, nor was there an *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*.
However, until the time of King Vasabha (609–653), these [works] were well-known...
The expositions, arguments, and foundational cases of the Sīhaḷika Theras are also found in these [works].
Furthermore, the composition of the commentaries on the Abhidhamma consists of the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the *Sammohavinodanī*, and the commentary on the five treatises beginning with the *Dhātukathā*.
At the request of the bhikkhu Buddhaghosa, who composed the *Sotatthakī* treatise under a name identical to his own, he produced three commentaries on the Abhidhamma.
For it is said therein: “By one of purified conduct and virtue, Possessing subtle and stainless intelligence;”
“By the bhikkhu Buddhaghosa, who was earnestly requested [to compose it]”—this is the introductory discourse on the commencement of the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.

And: “This commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, called the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, was composed by the Elder who bears the name Buddhaghosa as given by his teachers”—this is the concluding discourse of the *Aṭṭhasālinī*.
“At the request of the ascetic Buddhaghosa— of steady virtue,
unerring gait, and keen intelligence— I have composed this commentary on the meanings,
which I undertook to write for the purpose of elucidating those meanings that are most subtle.”
“Because it dispels delusion, it is called the *Sammohavinodanī*,” says the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, along with its concluding remarks:
“This is the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga* named the *Sammohavinodanī*, composed by the Elder whose name was accepted by his teachers as Buddhaghosa. This concludes the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding these three [commentaries], however, there is no specific mention of the name of the *Pañcappakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*, nor is an "entreator" (āyācaka) mentioned;
it appears as if that [commentary] was composed solely by the Master Buddhaghosa, impelled by his own faith alone.
For this is stated in its conclusion:
“Relying on the distinctions between wholesome and other states, and expanding upon them through various methods and manifold enumerations,
the Teacher proclaimed the seventh treatise of the Abhidhamma,
which he called the *Paṭṭhāna*, having established it with a well-arranged conclusion.”
"And that commentary which has been undertaken by me out of faith, [is now completed].
Thus far,
the Lord taught the Abhidhamma consisting of the seven treatises.
“This commentary on the entire [work] of that God of Gods among gods, which [was composed] formerly in the world of the gods, is now finished. Thus it begins.
It was composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa, a name accepted by his teachers.
"This is the commentary on the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka," thus it begins.

However, some modern elders say: "The commentaries on the Abhidhamma were composed by a certain elder—such as Saṅghapāla, Buddhamitta, Jotipāla, or others—at the request of Ācariya Buddhaghosa. This is their deliberation regarding the *Aṭṭhasālinī* and the *Sammohavinodanī*.
“Having been requested by Buddhaghosa, he did so,” thus it was stated by the author of the *Ganthakāra*.

From this it is known that the composer of the *Tīkā* was one person, whereas Master Buddhaghosa was merely the individual who made the request for them. And in the commentaries on the *Āgamas*, Master Buddhaghosa [states]:
“The discourse on virtue, the ascetic qualities, all the meditation subjects... pe...”
"Since all this has been very thoroughly explained by me in the *Visuddhimagga*, I shall not further analyze it here.
(Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā 1, Introduction) — By the word "by me," it is shown that the discourse on virtue and so forth was composed by himself in the *Visuddhimagga*. However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*—
“All meditation subjects, the [temperamental] conduct, the direct knowledges, and insight—all this has been explained here in the *Visuddhimagga*.

(Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā, Introduction to the Text) The phrase “Thus have I heard” (*evam me sutaṃ*) is stated here without the mention of the speaker. From this it is known that the author of the *Visuddhimagga* is one person, and the author of the *Abhidhamma-ṭīkā* is another.

"another. Although in the Abhidhamma commentaries the author Buddhaghosa is addressed by the venerable Thera using only these general terms of merit—"bhikkhu" and "yati"—and not by a term expressing respectful merit such as "thera," nevertheless, he is also addressed with these terms of superior merit:
"by him of purified conduct and virtue, of subtle and stainless intellect," and "by him of unhindered progress and excellent wisdom."
Because of this praise, it can be understood that he was indeed the teacher Buddhaghosa, the author of the *Visuddhimagga* and other works.
For from the very time of his full ordination (*upasampadā*), he was skilled in composition and endowed with the quality of proficiency in the scriptures (*pariyatti*);
and at that time, he would have been less than ten years [in seniority]. Therefore, it can be understood that he was not referred to as "the Elder" (*thera*).
But that is merely their excessive deliberation. For it cannot be taken that the Elder Ācariya Buddhaghosa was "under ten years of age" at that time;
for even in the conclusion of the *Visuddhimagga*, there is the statement:

"by the Elder whose name was accepted by his teachers as 'Buddhaghosa'," and neither [is there a statement] such as "by one of pure conduct and virtue, of subtle and stainless intelligence," nor "by one of unsluggish gait."
It is sufficiently praised by this much alone—by these two pairs of qualities—as when one says: "The sun has arisen, having eclipsed the light of the firefly.
For indeed, in the conclusions of his own compositions, the Teacher [Buddhaghosa] himself wrote:
"By him who is adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy, and who is endowed with a multitude of virtues such as virtue, conduct, speed, and gentleness..."
"By one endowed with the analytical power of wisdom capable of penetrating and plunging into both his own tradition and the traditions of others;

by a great expositor whose unimpeded radiance of knowledge [shines] upon the Teacher’s Dispensation, consisting of the Three Piṭakas along with their commentaries"—with such words, his own appropriate qualities were proclaimed. And he himself, having condensed the ancient Sinhalese commentaries...
He was the pioneer and the first author of the new commentaries (*abhinava-aṭṭhakathā*);
other authors of new commentaries, however, followed him and composed only one or two remaining commentaries.

Furthermore, regarding the commentaries on the Abhidhamma, whatever matter was stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, he took that very matter from it and inserted it in the appropriate place exactly as it was.

It has been stated. In particular, however, this matter is very clearly evident in the commentaries on the Vibhaṅgas of Dependent Origination, the Aggregates, the Bases, and the Elements, as well as in the commentaries on the Truths and the Discourses on Jhāna.
Furthermore, even where a slight difference in commentary is seen—amounting to only a few points—that which differs from the *Visuddhimagga* follows the opinion of the Abhidhammikas.
It should be understood that it is stated exactly as it was stated in the ancient *Aṭṭhakathā*.

And just as in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* an extended application (*atidesa*) to the *Samantapāsādikā*, the Vinaya commentary, is seen regarding the discussion on the unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*),
so too in the *Samantapāsādikā* an extended application to the *Aṭṭhasālinī* is likewise seen.
Furthermore, if the *Aṭṭhasālinī* were composed by another person, how could mutual cross-references between them be possible?

Therefore, the one who requested [the work] in the Abhidhamma commentaries was Buddhaghosa; however, the author of the *Sotatthakī* (the *Manorathapūraṇī*)—who has been accepted by the lineage of teachers down to the present day as "Cūḷabuddhaghosa," sharing the same name as the Master—is indeed someone else, and not the Venerable Master Mahā-Buddhaghosa.
Therefore, it is stated there as both "by a bhikkhu" and "by a yati.
However, if one does not reach a conclusion with this much alone, it should be investigated in this way:
when the elders such as Saṅghapāla and others were entreating the Elder Buddhaghosa to compose the *Visuddhimagga* and other works, did they [request it] for themselves...
Is it those who are more capable who pray, or those who lack faith? It is evident that it is precisely those with faith who pray.
And that being so, why would the Venerable Master Buddhaghosa—being himself more capable than others—pray to another?
For one endowed with faith, endowed with strength, and endowed with youth [does not need to do so].
It would be a heavy burden for the Teacher to compose a more excellent commentary on the Abhidhamma.
Furthermore, the words spoken in the Abhidhamma commentaries are identical in form to the explanatory passages spoken in the Visuddhimagga and the commentaries on the Āgamas.
If another were to compose the Abhidhamma commentary, there would somehow be a discrepancy in the form of those words.

It must indeed be so. Furthermore, by the statement shown in the conclusion of these works—“composed by the Elder who was given the name Buddhaghosa by his teachers”—it becomes evident that they were composed by Ācariya Buddhaghosa alone and not by anyone else.
Even those who claim they were composed by another are unable to definitively identify them as having been made by "this specific Elder."
Furthermore, not even a trace of evidence is found to show that [the Abhidhamma commentaries] were composed by another. Therefore, one must conclude this:

even in the case of the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā, it was the very same venerable teacher Mahā-Buddhaghosa—the author of the Visuddhimagga, the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā, and the Āgama-aṭṭhakathās—who, at the request of the monk named Buddhaghosa (who is now designated by teachers as "Cūḷa-Buddhaghosa"), composed it. This is the final conclusion to be reached here.

However, as for what is stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa* with the intention that "the teacher Buddhaghosa composed the *Aṭṭhasālinī* while still residing in Jambudīpa, prior to his arrival in the island of Sīhaḷa":
"225. He made the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the girdle of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*," that does not accord with the *Aṭṭhasālinī* as it is seen today. For in that [work], right at the beginning of the composition...
Having referred by way of analogy to the *Visuddhimagga*, both that work and the *Samantapāsādikā* are subsequently referred to in many places.
Therefore, it is exceedingly clear that after the Master arrived on the island of Sri Lanka,
he composed the *Visuddhimagga* and the *Samantapāsādikā*, and only afterwards [wrote the present work].
Regarding the composition of the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* commentary:
the Elder Ācariya Buddhaghosa, being requested by the Elder Soṇa, composed this Pātimokkha commentary named the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*,
based on the method of the Sinhalese Pātimokkha commentary which follows the oral tradition of the Mahāvihāra residents, without omitting even a single word.
He composed this work without contradicting either the Pāli Canon or the ancient commentaries of the Mahāvihāravāsins. Therefore, it is said in that commentary:
“By one who is gentle, free from agitation, Living with purity and austerity;”
Requested by the Elder Soṇa, who was endowed with discipline and conduct,
this commentary on him— complete in its analysis— is for the purpose of resolving the doubts of those monks who have conceived uncertainty therein.

“I shall recite, by name, the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, the beautiful [work] of the Mahāvihāravāsins, based on the lineage of the oral tradition. Thus ends the section on the eight doubts (*kaṅkhā*) and the introductory discourse on the composition of the treatise.
“I have undertaken this entire work according to the method of the Sinhalese commentaries (*sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā*).”
Relying upon the tradition of the recitation-lineage of the Mahāvihāravāsins,
this work has reached its conclusion, having taken up in its entirety the essence of all the commentaries and the entire meaning of the canonical texts.

"There is no passage here that would contradict the Canon (pāḷi) or the ancient commentaries (porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā) of the Mahāvihāravāsins"—this is the resolution of doubt. This concludes the concluding discourse.
Thus ends the composition of the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*.
There are also three other commentaries: the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*.
According to the conclusions found within them, these are known to have been composed by the Master Buddhaghosa himself.
However, certain statements expressed therein do not conform to the manner in which they are stated in the commentaries on the canonical scriptures (*Āgama*). Therefore, some...
They say, "This is the work of the teacher Buddhaghosa.
However, some maintain that these [commentaries] may have been first composed by the supporting theras and later brought to completion by the teacher through the process of revision and correction;
or else, they may have been composed by Cūḷabuddhaghosa, who requested the Abhidhamma commentary.
Whether it be so or otherwise, it is not easy at this point to determine it with absolute certainty. Therefore, we shall clarify this here by means of the concluding words of those [commentaries].
For among them, the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* was transmitted orally in the Siṃhala language while residing in the palace of King Sirikūṭa (Sirikuḍḍa), as requested by the Elder Kumārakassapa.

Having transposed the established ancient commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) into the Pāli language, having condensed the verbose sequence of words, and having provided commentary on the phrases and syllables not previously commented upon in the verses, he composed it. For it is said there, at the beginning of the work:
"The subtle commentary on its meaning, which has been handed down through successive tradition..."
That which was established on the island of Tambapaṇṇi in the language of the island...
[and so forth] ...I, having been earnestly requested by the Elder Kumārakassapa, whose mind is steadfast and who desires the endurance of the True Dhamma... [and so forth].
Having abandoned that discourse which had become overly prolix and its sequential arrangement of words,
and having composed a beautiful string of verses,
whatever of the phrasing and wording of those stanzas was not previously elucidated therein—
"Having analyzed that [work] alone, I shall explain the rest in another language, as it is identical in meaning"—
thus it is said in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, in the introduction to the book.
And in the conclusion, it is stated:
“In the monastery built by the grateful Adhirāja, while I was dwelling in the palace of King Sirikūṭa. (Dharmapada-aṭṭhakathā 2, Concluding Statement).
And here, in the conclusion of the *Samantapāsādikā*, it is stated that the one named Sirikūṭa is none other than King Mahānāma, who is called Siripāla.

They say thus. This being so, it should be understood that she performed this act while residing in the Dhūmarakkha-pabbata monastery, which had been granted by that king for the purpose of bringing [the relics] and encouraging their acceptance. For this is stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa*:
“In the places called Lohadvāra, Ralaggāma, Koṭipassa, and Āvana;”
Having had three monasteries built for the bhikkhus at Abhayuttara,
and having had a monastery constructed on Mount Dhūmarakkha,
he sent them to the bhikkhus who follow the Theravāda by means of his chief queen.
Furthermore, it is impossible to determine exactly when it was completed during that king's reign.
For he had it finished in the twenty-first year of that king's reign, and that king passed away in the twenty-second year.

Within this interval, it took a little more than one year to complete [the work], consisting of "the four commentaries on the Āgamas, the three commentaries on the Abhidhamma, and this commentary on the Dhammapada."
"All these cannot be brought to completion.

Thus, the author of the commentary *Paramatthajotikā* composed this commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha* and the *Suttanipāta*, named *Paramatthajotikā*, entirely according to his own wish, without being requested by anyone. For it is said at the beginning of the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā*:
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, the most worthy of veneration,
I shall compose a commentary on the meaning of some of the Minor Works (Khuddaka).
Although it is exceedingly difficult due to the profundity of the Minor Works, [I shall proceed].
This commentary on the teaching by one such as I is for those who have not yet awakened to it.
Nevertheless, even today the determination of the ancient teachers remains unbroken;
for the ninefold teaching of the Teacher stands exactly as it was.
Therefore, relying upon both the Teaching and the ancient exegesis, I desire to compose this commentary on the meaning;
it is out of great reverence for the True Dhamma, and not from a desire for self-exaltation.
“Listen with concentrated minds to that which is not for the purpose of disparaging others.
However, many discerning scholars, having examined these introductory verses (*ārambhagāthā*), say:
“This does not sound like the speech of the teacher, the Elder Buddhaghosa. This is their manner of examination: for the teacher Buddhaghosa—whatever [he wrote]...
He composed certain texts only when requested by others endowed with virtues such as moral discipline; however, in this case, there was no requester at all.

Furthermore, the Teacher made a formal promise, saying: "I shall compose [this] by translating the ancient Sinhalese commentaries," and "I shall compose it based on the recensional tradition of the Mahāvihāravāsins."

[He] does so; however, in this case, there is no such admission. Furthermore, the Teacher did not mention the difficulty of undertaking the commentaries on the four extremely profound Āgamas and the Abhidhamma;
yet here, by declaring his own lack of realization of the Dispensation with the words, "by one like me who has not awakened to the Dispensation," he states that [the task] is "exceedingly difficult."
He says this. Therefore, some say, "This is not the word of Master Buddhaghosa. That appears reasonable;
for in the conclusions of his own compositions, the Master declared his own power of knowledge with the words:
"By the unimpeded power of my knowledge regarding the Teacher’s Dispensation, which is divided into the three Piṭakas of scripture together with the commentaries. He [says]: "The Dispensation..."
"One such as I, lacking awakening, would find it exceedingly difficult"—one should certainly not speak such words.
Regarding the composition of the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, they say that the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā* was also composed by the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa alone; however, the reason for this is as follows:

It is not seen [in other sources]. However, it was composed by three elders—namely, the elder Atthadassi, the elder Buddhamitta, and the Mahīṃsāsaka elder Buddhadeva—at the request of those residing in the Mahāvihāra, following their method of recitation.
It has no specific name; for it is stated at its commencement:
“Having been requested by the Elder Atthadassi, who desired the long endurance of this *Buddhavaṃsa*, he approached him—
[the Elder] who dwells in non-association and always lives in purity.”
Likewise, by the wise Buddhamitta,
whose mind was tranquil and who was well-versed in the methods within the Mahīṃsāsaka lineage,
and similarly by the monk Buddhadeva, possessed of pure intelligence.
The commentary on the meaning of this Jātaka, which illuminates the inconceivable power of the Great Beings' deeds,
follows the oral tradition of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.
"I shall speak; may the virtuous ones grasp it well as I speak.

Up to this point, the manner in which the *Visuddhimagga* was composed together with all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)—which are well known for their status as the works of the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa Thera—is explained in detail.
[It is] the cause for the spreading of the entire world.
Is the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) renowned throughout the entire world? Yes, because it is based upon the perfectly pure Piṭaka scriptures;
because it encompasses the three trainings; because it is a linguistic adaptation of the ancient commentaries; because it avoids the tenets of other systems; because it clarifies our own system;
and because it provides a complete and detailed analysis of the categories of virtue, the ascetic practices, serenity, direct knowledge, wisdom, and so forth.
Because it elucidates the method of practice up to Arhatship; because it is composed of clear and unconfused words and phrases;

because its meaning is easy to understand; and because it demonstrates numerous hundreds of virtues—such as illustrating the bases capable of inspiring confidence and inducing followers to adopt the right view—it has become renowned throughout the entire world.
For this *Visuddhimagga* proceeds solely by relying upon the perfectly pure Piṭaka-Canon as established in the three councils;
it does not rely on the Canon of the seventeen schools such as the Mahāsaṅghika, nor on the Canon of the Mahāyānists.

Furthermore, the Three Trainings, together with their attendants, are presented here having been fully included. Indeed, this was stated by the Teacher at the commencement of his commentaries on the Āgamas:
“The virtues, the ascetic practices, and all the meditation subjects;
the detailed exposition of the meditative absorptions together with the methods of conduct;
all the direct knowledges, and the compendium of the calculation of wisdom;”
The aggregates, elements, bases, and the four noble faculties;
the truths, the mode of conditions, and the teaching with its perfectly pure and subtle methods;
the lineages of liberation, the paths, and the cultivation of insight.
"Since all of this has been explained by me with great clarity in the *Visuddhimagga*, I shall not analyze it further here.
Furthermore, since the *Visuddhimagga* was composed as a supplement to the commentaries on the four Āgamas, therefore those...
This was composed by way of translating the language of the ancient Sinhalese commentaries,
by way of condensing meanings that have been repeated, by way of avoiding the systems of others, and by way of illustrating our own system—
which is known as the pure determination of the Mahāvihāra dwellers. For this has been stated by the Teacher:
“Then, having set aside the delightful Sinhalese language,
I composed [this work] in a faultless language suited to the method of the *Tanti*,
not transgressing the tradition of the Elders who are lamps for the lineage of the Theras.”
“Having abandoned the matter that has come up again and again, I shall clarify the meaning for those who dwell in the Mahāvihāra and are skilled in subtle discernment. (Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā,
Introduction to the Text) “For this *Visuddhimagga* stands in the midst of all four Āgamas;”
"Having stood [there], he will clarify the meaning as it was spoken therein.

For this very reason, having taken that [text] together with this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), understand the meaning dependent upon the *Dīgha* [Nikāya]. Thus ends the introductory discourse on the composition of the work. (Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā, Introduction)
For this work has been completed by taking the essence from the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*),
according to the recitation-sections (*bhāṇavāra*) of the eighty-one-fold Pāḷi.
The *Visuddhimagga* itself consists of fifty-nine recitation-sections.
“Since it was composed for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the Āgamas,
therefore, together with that [commentary], the Aṭṭhakathā,
when counted by recitation sections (bhāṇavāra), is exactly one hundred and forty [sections] in its well-measured and defined extent. Thus ends the concluding discourse of the Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā.

If this *Visuddhimagga* had been composed by the Master solely through the power of his own knowledge, without having produced it like the commentaries on the scriptures (*āgama-ṭīkā*) and without consulting the ancient Sinhalese commentaries,
it would not have to be regarded as a constituent part of those scriptural commentaries;
rather, it would simply be said that "the scriptural commentaries are the essence of the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*)."
"Furthermore, the *Visuddhimagga* is not its essence; it was composed solely through the teacher’s own intelligence"—this is how one should speak.

However, since it was not composed in that manner, but rather in the very mode previously described, this *Visuddhimagga* too was composed according to the method of composing those commentaries on the Āgamas. For this very reason, [it is said] regarding the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*:
And it should be regarded as being the very essence. However,

some discerning individuals [have observed] that certain specific discourses on the Dhamma presented by the teacher Buddhaghosa in his works— without relying on ancient texts, but rather conjecturing through his own knowledge alone—
are similar to those shown by monks such as Assaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and Vasubandhu, who followed the Uttarapakkha school.
Seeing this, those with dissatisfied minds say: "We do not see the production of new books by Buddhaghosa through the power of his own knowledge alone, without depending on others.
Although these words of theirs are actually a form of censure, they turn out to be nothing but praise for the Theravādins.
For the Theravādins understand it thus: "By the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha himself..."
The Dhamma is to be taught and the Vinaya is to be laid down; they have been taught and laid down without remainder.
That very Dhamma-Vinaya is to be practiced as appropriate by monks endowed with faith and by householders alike;
no other Dhamma-Vinaya should be conjectured or sought after. However, if another Dhamma-Vinaya were [taught] by anyone...
If it were taught by relying on mere reasoning, that would be the teaching of that very reasoner, not the teaching of the Teacher. However,
whenever a word or phrase in the Blessed One’s Dhamma and Vinaya is unclear in its meaning, there, in each such instance, the ancient masters of the commentaries—
who were endowed with the qualities of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and who understood the Blessed One’s intention— [have explained it].
“The meaning should be grasped according to the method of exposition, not by means of one’s own arbitrary interpretation.
And Ācariya Buddhaghosa was one of those Theravādins; he too knows it in that very way. And this was said by the Master:
“The Dhamma and the Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha...”
He who was likewise known by his sons— those by whom,
in former times, they composed commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) after having abandoned their own opinions.
Therefore, having set aside whatever has been stated in the commentaries that is due to negligence,
[one should follow] everything [else] for those who possess reverence for the trainings.
Since this is the standard for the wise here,
therefore, having set aside other languages and having condensed the detailed path... [etc.]
"Since this commentary will also come to be, it should therefore be studied with care. Thus ends the eighth [chapter], the Introduction to the Text.
Therefore, the Teacher, without relying on the Dhamma and Vinaya of the Blessed One or the ancient commentaries, by means of his own knowledge—
Having relied upon or having taken up the worldly texts familiar to him, he did not compose any book whatsoever.
Had he, however, composed such a work, the Theravādins would have declared it—according to the method stated in the Mahāpadesa Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 2.188;
