Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.180)—that "surely this is neither the word of the Blessed One nor [the word] of the Elder Buddhaghosa."

They would surely discard it as "misapprehended. However, since this *Visuddhimagga* was composed by the Master through the mere transposition of the language of the ancient commentaries and so forth, for that very reason the Theravādins accept it—according to the method stated in the *Mahāpadesa Sutta*—thinking:
"This is certainly the word of the Blessed One, and it has been well-apprehended by the Elder Master Buddhaghosa."
Therefore, the path to the lower realms is spread throughout the entire world.
Furthermore, the classification of the factors of virtue (*sīla*) and the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), as well as the exposition of the method of practice, is already well-known.

Likewise, this *Visuddhimagga* is well-composed through its clearly intelligible words and sentences, as well as its unconfused words and sentences, in accordance with the style of the Canon (*pāḷi*).
Because it is well-constructed, its meaning is likewise easy to understand.

Therefore, wise people of pure aspiration, as they contemplate it, experience a measureless joy and gladness from moment to moment, being both sensitive to the meaning (*atthapaṭisaṃvedin*) and sensitive to the Dhamma (*dhammapaṭisaṃvedin*).
In this regard, there are many inspiring accounts that bring forth confidence, such as the story of the Elder Mahātissa and others. 1.15 Sīhaḷa Vatthus (Sinhalese Stories)
Furthermore, the stories of the Elder Sāriputta—the General of the Dhamma—and others, as well as the sites in Jambudīpa, have been illuminated.
Upon seeing these and recollecting them, a powerful faith arises in noble persons, and a desire to follow in their footsteps arises, thinking: "When indeed shall we ourselves become like this?"
Thus, it should be understood that this *Visuddhimagga* has become renowned throughout the entire world due to its many hundreds of virtues,
such as its reliance on the perfectly pure Piṭaka texts. And just as this *Visuddhimagga*,

so too other commentaries on the Tipiṭaka composed by the Master have likewise become renowned throughout the entire world for their virtues, such as being translations of the ancient commentaries into different languages.
Furthermore, by this much, the meaning of questions such as "For what purpose was this done? has also been explained in detail.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Of the one worthy of esteem, for the wise..."
For him whose steadfast mind is not intoxicated,
whose radiant qualities such as wisdom have arisen like playful splendors,
he shines in the world for the joy of the virtuous.
That man of firm and keen intellect named Buddhaghosa,
having been deeply honored by the learned,
took [the work] born of its own nature and acquired through his own skill and effort.
The voice of Subuddha, as if bestowing glory,
[proclaimed]: "When the Supreme Buddha had attained Parinibbāna,
in the tenth century of years..."
"Born," thus was he known by the wise as the sprout of the Buddha’s lineage,
possessing the full measure of maturity; he is the knower,
the sage, the foremost among the noble-born.
He was born in the southern region,
in the delightful Indiya, that mine of virtuous people;
he became the lord of those who sought the true goal.
He was born there in the village of Moraṇḍa,
rightly descended from a noble family of the Puññānita clan;
for the sake of bringing about the welfare of the world, he was born to a hero.
Like the first ray of the rising sun,
his intellect having grown, he reached full maturity and brought joy to the circle of his kinsmen and the gods alike.
He attained proficiency without effort in the Vedas,
the sciences, and other treatises on various crafts,
through his pure resolve and discernment.
Discerning that "this is the essence" and "this is the non-essence," he understood the non-essence within the Vedas; therefore,
he did not find satisfaction in that learning.
For him who was seeking the praised essence,
the essence of the True Dhamma was obtained through hearing;
like a valley, he inclined toward the Buddha’s dispensation.
Having become resolute there for the sake of departing,
that seeker of the Dhamma shone forth there,
as if having already attained the going-forth and full ordination.
There was the Elder Upasankamma Visuddha,
whose wisdom was renowned within the Vādī Nikāya;
for at that time, they resided in Dakkhiṇāpatha.
The residents, born of the Theriya lineage,
as well as the Sage who speaks otherwise, proclaim the doctrine of the Lord of Sages according to their respective attainments.
In order to further attain the essence of the true Dhamma,
she collected the Pāḷi spoken by the Victor;
the play of her tongue was directed by her mind.
Dwelling in merit like a goddess, he shone forth.
Thus, having correctly understood that "this is the one-way path to complete purification," he grasped it firmly.
The path for the attainment of turning away (*vivaṭṭa*)—
for that purpose, he entered into supreme application (*yoga*).
Great is his natural wisdom and his teaching.
Vast knowledge was not found by him elsewhere;
therefore, when he had crossed the ocean known as "Buddha," they recognized his power in accomplishing what was difficult to achieve.
The fame of the Buddha, a well-praised sound, shall prevail;
his teachers were highly learned.
They gave him the name "Buddha," which is endowed with meaning.
Ghosoti [was the name of the village] of the Perfectly Enlightened One Mataṅgagata.
He resided in the town called Mayūradūta,
as well as in Kañjīvha, Pura, and other places.
How did he of concentrated mind grasp that which was called the "Andhaka" teaching, consisting of eight sections,
from that wise one [Sumedha] to such an extent?
When his mind was thus satisfied,
there arose within him an even greater desire to fully understand the ultimate meaning of the words of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The commentaries, together with their sub-commentaries,
which were brought [to Ceylon] by the eminent masters beginning with Mahāmahinda,
along with the Theravāda and its well-determined expositions—
Then, alas, Laṅkā shone forth.
Knowing this occurrence, he thought:
"What if I were to go to that delightful Laṅkā?"
Having approached, one should study this great commentary which adorns the mine of jewels;
let it be recited and composed in the Sinhalese language.
"Having composed this new string of verses,
I shall thus accomplish the welfare of those who consider themselves Buddhas in other lands."
And that pure teaching which had come to Laṅkā,
like the spotless moon freed from frost and other obscurations,
shone forth; at that time, no other doctrine—
The lineage of humans attained the state of non-lineage.
For within a hundred years after the Jina had passed into Nibbāna,
those belonging to the Dispensation were in harmony.
In the teaching of the Jina, there were those of like doctrine,
and at that time no dissension whatsoever arose.
Later, however, when the trees of the True Dhamma were struck down—
Dependent upon those phenomena and winds that have arisen as evils,
with a mind filled with agitation,
they applied themselves with firm diligence.
Chantings should be performed well by those who are skillful and firm,
even when being restrained strongly;
for even trees that have been cut down may grow back again.
Some indeed treated the Dhamma and Vinaya otherwise than you;
they formed various factions with many different doctrines,
creating factions within the teaching of the Conqueror.
Purifying themselves through other debates uttered by the Jinas,
they [expound] the Vinaya and the Dhamma; their debates,
their debaters, and their Piṭakas— these are [the means].
They came to adorn Laṅkā as if it were their own home;
they accepted [the invitation], but those dwelling in the great and famous monasteries, such as Abhayagiri and others, did not.
Just as the Pāḷi was spoken by the Buddha and its essential meaning was understood by the masters,
so too [the teaching] did not deviate from that, according to the pure elders.
There arose some dispute concerning the words "Vādī" and "Vivādī.
They protected the Sthavira doctrine as if it were their own life,
along with its system, its meaning, and its definitive conclusions.
Therefore, it is impossible for those who speak otherwise than that to refute or even approach this path.
And I consider the fear of the disruption of that teaching [to be the reason].
“Even at times difficult to cross, they were held together by the threads of fear;
through delusion and other such states, they would exist”— having inscribed this upon a book, they preserved it correctly.
For at that time, in order to ward off their objections,
the Sage Buddhaghosa, a bearer of the Victor’s Dispensation, possessed of sharp intelligence and skillful wisdom, [taught] the training known as the Raṇavivāda.
You have gone to the excellent island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Having reached Laṅkā, you are like one who has reached the firm,
certain further shore for crossing the ocean of the Great Commentary.
Residing there in the Mahāvihāra, the noble abode of his pure lineage, he shone like the rising moon adorning the sky; and there,
in the southern region, he dwelt as a master.
The virtuous lord of the great city, who had practiced the Dharma with purity, built a magnificent palace known as Sobha,
which was recognized as a monastery and served by noble people.
She practiced the yoga correctly, having approached the lineage of the Elders such as Buddhamitta and others,
whose traditions were unimpaired; she was attended by him,
whose wisdom was awakened through various modes of knowledge.
Having seen with his wisdom that the meaning was laid bare—
without omission— in the commentaries on the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya,
both in its own context and in other contexts, as if it were open before him;
The Elders, who had reached the path of the Victor’s unity and were established in the deathless,
considered him as exceedingly difficult to find as a rare jewel.
Having understood the meaning of the Dhamma and Vinaya for the sake of granting whatever was desired—
This work, titled *Cintāmaṇi*, is the very embodiment of well-discerned wisdom; it is that which the supreme Elder Kavisaṅghapāla,
whose mind was firmly resolved therein, composed for the benefit of the people.
“Although there exist various treatises on practice,
some of them do not follow the Buddha’s intention;
they are also in contradiction with the traditions of the pure Elders.”
Therefore, let him compose a pure treatise on practice.
May he dwell amidst the grove of the waters of loving-kindness and other virtues upon the soil of humanity,
following the path of conduct that leads to the goal and away from what is not the path.
"For the sake of purification"— thinking, "I shall fulfill the hopes of the elders who have made this aspiration"— he of purified wisdom,
whose mind was joined with heroism and compassion, composed the *Visuddhimagga*.
Having thoroughly grasped and taken up the commentary on the *Khila* (the "Stumps"),
which is continuous and essential, he has composed this work with great care,
disregarding even his own weariness; what wise person would not find it pleasing?
